The European Union has adopted sanctions against Kremlin assets used for disinformation and information manipulation.

Following the announcement made by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Sunday, the Council of the European Union has decided to suspend, as of today, the EU-wide distribution of the state-run disinformation channels Russia Today and Sputnik, the European Commission said.
President Von der Leyen said: in these times of war, words matter.
We are witnessing mass propaganda and misinformation about this outrageous attack on a free and independent country.
We will not allow Kremlin apologists to spew their toxic lies justifying Putin's war, nor to sow the seeds of division in our Union.
High Representative and Vice-President Josep Borel said: the Kremlin is systematically using information manipulation and disinformation as an operational tool in its attack on Ukraine.
It also poses a significant and direct threat to public order and the security of the Union.
Today, we are taking an important step to stop Putin's manipulative operations and end the proliferation of state-controlled Russian media in the EU.

Earlier we have already imposed sanctions on the leadership of RT, including the editor-in-chief Simonyan, and it is only logical that the activities that organisations carry out within our Union should also be sanctioned.
"Russia Today" and "Sputnik" play an essential and fundamental role in furthering Russia's aggression against Ukraine and in supporting this aggression.
This poses a significant and direct threat to public order and EU security.

Both media are involved in coordinated efforts to manipulate information, including disinformation, as documented since 2015 by the EU Task Force for Strategic Communication with the Eastern Neighbourhood of the European External Action Service.

In view of the gravity of the situation and in response to Russia's actions to destabilise the situation in Ukraine, it is necessary and in accordance with fundamental rights and freedoms to introduce further restrictive measures and to suspend the television and radio broadcasting activities of Russia Today and Sputnik in or directed at the EU.
The sanctions cover all means of transmission and distribution, e.g. cable, satellite, IP TV, platforms, websites and apps.
All relevant licenses, permits and distribution arrangements have been suspended.
These measures cover all EU Member States and are directly applicable immediately.

Cooperation with and between the independent media regulators within the European Regulators Group for Audiovisual Media Services (ERGA) is essential to ensure swift implementation of measures by operators.

Some regulators have already taken concrete action to restrict Russian media involved in disinformation, information manipulation and interference in their respective territories under EU audiovisual media rules.
Context.

Several regulators in EU member states have already taken sanctions against state-controlled Russian broadcasters and channels involved in the ecosystem of disinformation and information manipulation (e.g. in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland), while Germany has banned the distribution of the German edition of Russia Today due to lack of a license.
The past year has seen an unprecedented crackdown on independent media in Russia.
Russian authorities have used draconian legislation - in particular the "foreign agents" law - to silence independent media and individual journalists deemed critical of the government.
Russian journalists have been threatened, persecuted and forced to flee the country just for doing their job.
This is unacceptable.
Freedom of access to information is a fundamental right enshrined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.
The EU will continue to support media freedom and pluralism everywhere.

The Constitutional Court annulled the text on the end of proportional voting - it is so vague that it is contrary to the rule of law

In today's decision, the Constitutional Court also takes a position on the provision in the Electoral Code that "the proportional electoral system for the election of deputies under Article 246 shall apply until the first regular election of deputies is held after the entry into force of this Law".
It was enshrined in § 64 of the Transitional and Final Provisions.
But the CC declared it unconstitutional.

The provision in question is a key one - it was proposed in the short 45th Parliament by There is Such a Nation in response to criticism that the party, which was formed to implement the will of the 2017 referendum, was not in a hurry to have a majority vote once it entered Parliament.
With this provision Slavi Trifonov's party confirmed that it has not given up the majority vote.
It is not serious to introduce a majority system overnight, said Iva Miteva of ITN, who was also chairwoman of the National Assembly.
That is why at the last moment Slavi Trifonov's people introduced an amendment in the transitional and final provisions, which means that the proportional electoral system is coming to an end.
The amendment was voted at the 14-hour session of the National Assembly before the Easter holidays.
Most of the debate on the text then passed under the sign of which of the two parties - "There is such a nation" and GERB more wants majority elections.
Thus, in the Electoral Code entered the prospect of abolishing the proportional electoral system, but without saying what replaces it.
When asked about the majority vote, Slavi Trifonov said in his interview for BNR in May: "In order to change the elections, to make them majority, there is work to be done to make it real.
We need to create 240 single-member districts, have a clear census, have a bunch of work done by different institutions.
Enough time has to pass, the will has to be there and it has to be realized.
It will happen when there is a parliament of calm and political will.
It is not enough to have the desire, you also need to have the capability and the necessary technology.
This thing will happen with all these conditions."

The Constitutional Court's reasoning for declaring the provision unconstitutional is interesting: "The provision is addressed to the next National Assembly, prescribing it to adopt new rules for holding parliamentary elections under an unspecified electoral system other than the proportional system within an unspecified period of time.
The provision is vague, contradictory and practically unenforceable, therefore it contradicts the principle of the rule of law, proclaimed in Art. 1 of the Constitution.

It seeks to abolish the application of the current proportional electoral system, without specifying what system should be introduced in order to make parliamentary elections possible in the first place.

Inasmuch as there is no indication of the system to be applied at the "first regular elections" - majority, mixed or other, and no such indication can be derived from the other texts of the IDIC Act, the meaning of the impugned provision cannot be ascertained.
The deadline for the implementation of the prescribed normative change is absolutely indefinite because it is linked to the holding of the "first regular elections".
The Basic Law does not divide elections into "regular" and "irregular", but only indicates the hypotheses in which new elections are necessary.
The use of a term that is not used in the Constitution or elsewhere in national electoral law makes the provision vague and contrary to the rule of law.
It therefore contradicts the principle of legal certainty as an element of the rule of law," the court's reasoning reads.

"The SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus was discovered in late 2019.

But what are the facts?
This viral genome is similar to the SARS-CoV coronavirus identified in 2002-2003, which is responsible for the SARS (severe acute respiratory syndrome) epidemic in the Far East.

This was explained by the Chairman of the Bulgarian Scientific Society of Pharmacy and Head of the Department of Pharmacology, Pharmacotherapy and Toxicology at the Faculty of Pharmacy of MU - Sofia prof.
Georgi Momekov, PhD, during a discussion on "Vaccines for COVID-19 through the prism of science", the press centre of the Ministry of Health reported.
In his words, this means that science has been working on prototypes of the vaccines we now use against COVID-19 for nearly 20 years.
"As for the iRNA vaccines, which are speculated to be not well known to medicine - that is not true either.
The use of iRNAs as therapeutic modalities and vaccines has been worked on since the 1990s," he said.

The forum, organized as part of the Ministry of Health's "+Me" information campaign to raise awareness about the benefits of vaccines and vaccination against COVID-19, was attended by 125 people working in 17 of the country's emergency care centers.

Prof. Prof. Georgi Momekov gave a brief overview of the vaccine production methodology, moving from vaccines containing live attenuated pathogen, through inactivated viral vaccines, classical subunit vaccines containing the corresponding viral antigen and adjuvant (substance that helps to generate an immune response), to informative RNA vaccines.
He explained the advantages of the iRNA vaccines.
On the one hand, they are safe because they do not contain a virus, bacteria or other disease-causing agent.
They contain neither mercury-containing preservatives nor aluminum-based adjuvants.
On the other hand, they are effective because they induce an adequate immune response, and most importantly, the iRNA technology allows vaccines to adapt rapidly to emerging variants.

"To people who talk about experimental liquids, I can say that there is nothing more defined than the composition of the products registered by the drug agencies." The professor supported his opinion with publicly available information on the qualitative and quantitative composition of the iRNA vaccines and the components included in them, including excipients.

Prof. Momekov also presented data on the tissue distribution of the respective vaccines and that the expression of viral proteins is temporary, with maximum detectable levels of spike proteins in the order of picograms/ml within 2-3 days after vaccination.
"All the components of vaccines break down in the human body in a few days without changing our DNA and affecting our reproductive abilities," Prof.
Momekov, drawing on post-marketing and cohort studies conducted in Canada, Israel, the EU and the US.

He also commented on the difference between natural and acquired immunity, or between so-called post-infectious and post-vaccinal immunity, presenting data from large-scale post-marketing surveillance from the US Centers for Disease Control demonstrating that the risk of reinfection with hospitalization is significantly higher in people relying on natural immunity.

As a conclusion, the professor pointed out, "The problem with SARS-CoV-2 is that this coronavirus is low-immunogenic and does not generate aggressive and durable immunity, which is why timely administration of a booster vaccine is important."
Regarding the safety profile of vaccines, Prof.
Momekov explained that side effects due to vaccination are always compared with the same effects occurring after the disease.

Current data strongly suggest that the risk of acute kidney injury, arrhythmias, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism is several times higher with COVID-19, whereas no such risk has been found with the iRNA vaccine.

How China is taking advantage of the pandemic
Why was China able to tackle the pandemic so quickly?
Is a dictatorial regime more successful?
The West is already sounding the alarm. "Deutsche Welle offers a commentary by Alexander Görlach*.
China's mask diplomacy since the beginning of the pandemic has turned into vaccine diplomacy.
For the second time in a year, the world is facing an acute shortage - first of protective masks and now of vaccines - as China's autocracy presents itself as the world's saviour and lends a hand.
But only the naive can assume that this is an expression of human compassion.
The truth is that in many world capitals - from Washington to Berlin - they are sounding the alarm.
Because the Chinese air bridge, through which vaccines are delivered - first to Serbia and now to Hungary - is a smart move by Beijing in the battle between systems.
Dictatorship - more successful in the pandemic?
According to the ideology of the Chinese nomenklatura, the People's Republic is doing so well in the pandemic only because there is neither party pluralism nor free elections in China.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping never tires of repeating how his party had defeated the virus with a mixture of Confucianism and "Chinese-style socialism".

Philosopher Tongdong Bai of Fudan University in Shanghai explains the superiority of the Chinese model: 'The weakness of Western democracies is that all adults have the right to vote in elections, which means they can have a say on issues they understand nothing about'.

This argument is also debated in the Western world - when there is a debate about whether governments should make their own decisions based on expert conclusions or whether they are obliged to consult parliaments as well.
In this regard, Bai advocates that democratic communities should be governed through elections only at the local level.
The more abstract the actions of a government, the more arguments there are for a meritocratic expert model of governance, which the Communist Party of China considers its trademark.

And the reality at the moment only confirms the Chinese theory: while in 2020 the economies of the free world countries suffered badly and unemployment rose dramatically, the People's Republic has long since recovered.

Even Donald Trump's four-year trade war with Beijing has not seriously weakened China: the willingness to invest in a country where 1 million people are imprisoned in the northwest - in concentration camps ringed with barbed wire and watchtowers - has not waned.
Chinese exports have recovered to their pre-pandemic levels and domestic consumption is growing.
China's "soft power".
For a long time, China could not counter anything to the American "soft power" and its achievements in the second half of the 20th century.
Soft power refers to methods and opportunities for exerting influence outside the realm of politics, including classical foreign policy.

In the case of the USA, it was mainly music and films that advertised the "American way of life" and alongside which there was a growing desire to learn English - all the way to the most remote parts of the world.
According to a German survey, however, in the last year of Donald Trump's term the popularity of the US has dropped and that of China has increased.
The People's Republic has acquired its own "soft power": masks and vaccines.
The mood could also turn in those countries around the world that the EU is currently neglecting because it is failing to tackle the pandemic even in its own member states.
In the US, things might improve a bit.
But they will also be dealing mostly with themselves - because of the incompetence of the previous president, the pandemic has done enormous damage.

If vaccines from Europe and North America are only available in countries where white people are in the majority, then people in other parts of the world will have to either wait or accept China's offer.

Then the "soft power" of the free world and the attractiveness of its democratic model will be weakened to previously unknown levels. * Alexander Görlach is a Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Council on the Ethics of International Relations and a Senior Research Fellow at the Institute for Religion and International Studies, University of Cambridge.

This geopolitical mish-mash we are seeing now will severely damage the EU and Bulgaria: much higher prices in Europe, very high profits for Russia and China.

Then also an inspection was carried out and there was no gas price for nearly two weeks.

Since then, the West has spent hundreds of billions of euros on eradicating terrorism.
But there are more jihadists in the world today than there were 20 years ago.

It was also the forerunner of the global jihad.
Sending the planes against the Twin Towers in New York on September 11, 2001.

(3,000 people died in that attack), he challenged America, humiliated the West, and instilled generations of jihadists with unshakable faith, even though he himself had to hide for the rest of his life.

Because Osama bin Laden was not content with just hitting the world's first power, but managed to drag the US into a war of attrition that could not be won, just as he had predicted, Colin Clark points out.

Bin Laden also understood the importance of turning war zones into training grounds for jihadists and invested his wealth in funding training for fighters for Afghanistan - in Chechnya, Bosnia, Somalia.
All his devoted servants who then fed his networks.

Some 80% of respondents said they had already been forced to make significant compromises, such as cutting back on travel (62%) or heating (47%), borrowing from friends or relatives (42%), finding a second job (40%) and skipping meals (29%).

Across the six countries, 64% say they "often" or "sometimes" can't decide what to cut anymore because they have already cut back to what they can, 28% say they have overspent by mid-month, and 27% often or sometimes fear losing their home.
On average, around 27% of respondents in the six countries describe their financial and material situation as "precarious", i.e.
"one unexpected expense can change everything", while 55% said they had to be careful.

For many, the future looks even worse: a majority of Europeans (55%) believe they face a very or somewhat significant risk of falling into uncertainty in the coming months, with one in five (17%) rating the possibility of this as very high.
Italians and Greeks are the most worried, with 70 and 68% of respondents respectively admitting to being very or somewhat concerned.
Some 47% of respondents in the UK think the risk of uncertainty is significant, as do 42% of those in France.

The tension was felt mostly by the parents. 72% across the six countries noted that they had cut back on their own leisure activities (76%), hair and beauty treatments (72%) and clothing budgets (72%) in order to preserve their children's quality of life.

Almost half of parents (48%) in the six countries admitted to regularly cutting back on food to feed their children, while 66% said they had been forced to limit children's activities, including outings and holidays.

The survey shows striking differences between countries on which groups are considered most at risk of falling into poverty: pensioners in Germany (61%), younger people in Italy (57%) and single-parent families in the UK (55%).

When Johann Sebastian Bach was composing Partita No. 2, he learned of the death of his wife Maria Barbara.
He then dedicated the last movement of this work to her.
The Chaconne!
I am currently studying this work intensively, working on it myself, reading up on the story and trying to come up with a coherent interpretation.
But first and foremost, it gives me comfort.
We all escape into music at one time or another.
We listen to them to escape the bitter reality, to amuse ourselves or to sort out our thoughts.
There are many things buzzing around in my head, touching me, making me angry and sad at the same time.
Bach's Chaconne helps me to organize these thoughts as I play his masterpiece.
At the beginning, Bach introduces the main theme in a D minor motif.
He spells out the name of his deceased wife again with the notes he uses.
You can feel the pain, the despair and helplessness.
At this moment, I am thinking of the sea of lights in front of St. Stephen's Cathedral, which commemorates the more than 5,000 people who have died in this pandemic.
Followed by a pianissimo, which symbolizes the lamentation of those who, despite a lack of support, fought against the death of these many people with very simple, only tenderly breathed notes.
Occasionally their pleading voices can be heard - but as in Bach's music, they are barely heard against the heavy chords of published opinion.
Bach then opens the performance.
It is the polyphony that gives this music meaning.
The struggle of sounds and words for weight.
The necessary discourse, combined with the freedom to say and write what is.
The contradiction that is supposed to fuel the necessary social progress.
The balancing of polyphonic currents.
And most importantly: What priority do content strands have?
Freedom, education, cohesion, physical and mental health and the need for democratic dissonance.
Or particular interests and a focus on themselves, but without considering the outcome of this work.
Time and again, Bach vehemently opposes the self-imposed rules.
However, he recaptures this resistance with Protestant toughness.
But the pain doesn't subside.
It ends in a wild arpeggio.
Chord cascades that have nothing playful about them, but rather foreshadow what is to come.
Many people feel and know that our democracy needs more dissent, more resistance and more journalistic freedom.
But how exactly in these times?
It ends in a tumult with heavy bass beats and leads into the initial theme.
The basic motif in D minor is transformed into a pleasant-sounding D major chord.
The chord decompositions reflect normality.
It is the embellished façade that can only be maintained for a few bars in Bach's Chaconne.
Because your own conscience is pushing you too hard.
He knows how things stand with him - we know how things stand with us.
The D major chord stands majestically, even presidential, at the beginning of the final section.
And a deep C is already mixed in between.
The presidential, even the clerical, wear out in these chords.
People die, are bitten by rats, lie in the dirt and find no way out.
Those on whom we base our hopes, however, find no or only insufficient words for these pre-Christmas tragedies.
Are they trapped in fatigue, indifference or even profane self-interest?
But Bach has a plan.
He shakes things up.
Lets the palaces and magnificent buildings of his music collapse and reduces himself to the essentials.
He only allows the interpreter to say the bare minimum.
No ornamentation, no accompanying chords, no pomp.
Instead, vehemence.
At the end an A ostinato with semitone steps.
It symbolizes a society torn apart.
Willfully destroyed by those who are harmed by harmony.
They need the state of emergency - thinking they are the center of attention.
Bach knew that this was not a permanent solution.
At the end he brings the chords together, softly dabbed, to a single note.
It ends at the low D.
Inner peace at last.
Or the calm before the storm.

The consequences are alarming and visible to all: every year, thousands of fish and birds die in agony from human plastic waste.
The European Union is now taking further action to reduce the gigantic quantities of waste.
For the protection of the oceans and animals, from 3.
The ban affects drinking straws, tableware, to-go cups and cutlery, as well as fast food packaging made of polystyrene.

But now a new problem is emerging: According to a study by European consumer protection associations, plastic-free disposable tableware made from cardboard, palm leaves or sugar cane often contains substances that are hazardous to health.
Every second plastic-free product contains harmful substances.
More than half (53 percent) of 57 products tested, such as straws, bowls and plates, contained undesirable substances above the recommended guideline value.
These include potentially carcinogenic substances such as 'eternal chemicals' that remain in the environment for many generations.
This is the conclusion of a study by the European Consumer Organization BEUC.

One dog year equals seven human years?
US researchers believe that the widespread rule of thumb regarding the age of dogs, according to which one year is roughly equivalent to seven human years, is quite wrong.

According to genetic analyses, the four-legged friends do not age at a consistently faster rate than their masters, write Trey Ideker from the University of California San Diego and his team in the journal "Cell Systems".
Instead, young dogs age particularly quickly compared to humans, but later the ageing process slows down.
New formula proposed.
Instead of the simple 7-year rule of thumb, the researchers propose a somewhat more complicated formula based on their studies of 104 Labrador retrievers: "Human age = 16 ln(dog age) + 31".
Accordingly, a one-year-old dog would not be comparable in age to a seven-year-old human, but to a 31-year-old human, and a four-year-old dog to a 53-year-old human.
At nine, a dog would then have reached the comparable human age of 66 years.
"ln" is the natural logarithm.
Mathematically, it ensures that a dog ages significantly faster in the first few years.
While the 7-year rule can lead to a very high dog age, even 21 years "only" corresponds to 80 dog years.
According to the 7-year rule, a dog would already be 147 years old at this point.
In their analysis, the researchers concentrated on tiny changes in the DNA.
These numerous DNA methylations occur in both humans and dogs.
The methylations form certain patterns in the genetic material that indicate the life phase of an individual.
The researchers took advantage of this and established a connection between the age-dependent patterns in dogs and those in humans.
They derived the new formula from their results.
Jogging with "dog pensioners" It is important to better understand the ageing process of dogs, said Ideker according to a press release from his university.
Veterinarians often still use the old 7-year rule of thumb and make diagnostic and therapeutic decisions dependent on it.
However, further studies are needed, the researchers write.
The new formula was only developed on the basis of the Labrador Retrievers studied.
For other dog breeds that have a lower or higher life expectancy, the formula may differ.
He now sees his own dog with different eyes, said Ideker.
"I have a six-year-old dog.
She still goes jogging with me, but I'm now realizing that she might not be quite as young as I thought."

For example, the lenticularis clouds, also known as lee clouds.
This celestial spectacle makes it look as if we are getting a visit from another universe, which is why people like to call the clouds flying saucers.

The supermoon rises - the most beautiful pictures of the celestial phenomenon
This is how the spectacular celestial phenomenon is created.
As lenticularis clouds tend to form on the leeward side of mountains, i.e. the side facing away from the wind, they are also known as leeward clouds.
They form when moist air flows over an obstacle, such as a hill or mountain.
The air often flows around individual mountains, but in the case of a mountain range aligned perpendicular to the wind direction, overflow becomes more and more likely with increasing wind speed.
This creates wave-like air movements on the leeward side.
This current is therefore also referred to as "lee waves".
The water vapor in the atmosphere makes this wave movement visible in the form of clouds.
According to experts from the German Weather Service (DWD), another prerequisite for the spectacular lee clouds is stable atmospheric stratification.
Unlike in a thunderstorm, the clouds do not rise upwards, but remain flat at their apex.
The best conditions for the formation of unusual clouds.
Spectacular lee clouds: a phenomenon that is not uncommon in Germany.
According to the weather portal wetter.net, lenticularis clouds do not move with the current, but remain stationary as long as the humidity and flow conditions do not change drastically.
Meteorologists can easily recognize a foehn weather situation from leeward clouds.
The unusual clouds are therefore often referred to as foehn clouds, foehn boats or foehn fish.

"It's a strange choice because (...) because of the war (in Ukraine) we have to deal with issues of war and peace," he added to journalists.
Orban is seeking a fifth term in office, the fourth in a row.
Opinion polls recently put his right-wing nationalist Fidesz party several percentage points ahead of the alliance of six opposition parties.
This is the first time it has competed in this form.
The alliance of left-wing, green, liberal and right-wing conservative parties wants to optimize its chances in this way.
The leading candidate of the opposition alliance, the independent conservative Peter Marki-Zay, called for the Orban government to be voted out in a Facebook video.
"Let's choose a better world, a happy Hungary," he said outside his home in the small south-eastern Hungarian town of Hodmezövasarhely, where he has been mayor since 2018.
He himself will go to the polls after attending the service, explained the professed Catholic.
Orban rages against the opposition.
The election is overshadowed by Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine.
In a final television interview on Saturday evening, Orban accused the opposition of wanting to interfere in the war in neighboring Ukraine.
"The left has made a pact with the Ukrainians, and if it wins, it will drag Hungary into the war," he said.
In fact, there is no such pact, and Orban presented no evidence of this.
The opposition alliance includes not only left-wing and social democratic parties, but also green, liberal and right-wing conservative parties.
Its leading candidate, 49-year-old Peter Marki-Zay, is a non-partisan conservative and an avowed Catholic.
Friendship with Putin.
Orban, in turn, has forged friendly relations with Russian President Vladimir Putin in recent years.
He only half-heartedly condemned the Russian war against Ukraine.
At the opposition's final rally in Budapest on Saturday evening, Marki-Zay accused the head of government of "treason" because of his stance on Moscow.
"We are all ashamed of Viktor Orban," he said.
"But now we are washing this shame away from us." Even before the war in Ukraine, Orban had been in permanent conflict with the EU.
In the course of his rule, he undermined democratic institutions, restricted media freedom and damaged the independence of the judiciary.
Critics also accuse him of corruption and misuse of EU funding.
Observers fear electoral fraud.
To remedy these shortcomings, the EU introduced a rule of law mechanism at the end of 2020.
Member states that violate the principles of the rule of law may have their funding withdrawn in future.

The EU Commission is already withholding funds earmarked for Hungary from the coronavirus recovery fund because the Orban government has not yet been able to credibly demonstrate that they have been used correctly.

Orban, who proclaimed "illiberal democracy" based on the Russian model in 2014, also changed the electoral laws in such a way that it is becoming increasingly difficult for political rivals to vote him out of office.
The way constituencies are drawn up and the voting rights for ethnic Hungarians in neighboring countries favor Orban's Fidesz party.
Orban also unabashedly put the resources of the government and the state at the service of Fidesz's election campaign.
According to election researchers, the Fidesz camp spent eight to ten times as much money on the election campaign as the opposition.
There are also fears of classic electoral fraud.

Legalizing the registration of bogus addresses and the photographing of ballot papers in the polling booth could encourage vote-buying and the shifting of voters to direct constituencies with narrow majorities.
Steinmeier's self-criticism: never look back
Federal President Steinmeier admits mistakes in his Russia policy.
An unusual admission.
Self-criticism is rare in politics.
He was wrong, Steinmeier said in the ZDF "Morgenmagazin" on Tuesday Photo: Michael Kappeler/dpa.
The Bundeswehr was in Afghanistan for 20 years.
The mission ended with the victory of the Taliban. In 2001, with some notable exceptions, the political class was firmly convinced that the military had to be sent to Afghanistan.
When the Bundeswehr withdrew, no responsible politician admitted that they had made a mistake in 2001.
Politicians usually follow the doctrine: forwards always, backwards never.
Even intellectually gifted politicians avoid critical retrospection, where there is obviously nothing to gain.
The disdain for mistakes is an astonishingly unique feature of the political establishment.
In modern management and in corporate headquarters, error culture is state of the art.
In complex, open processes that can never be fully predicted and controlled, errors of judgment are inevitable.
Therefore, those who recognize and correct mistakes are competent - and not those who make the audience believe that mistakes only happen to stupid people.
Although self-criticism is no longer a strict taboo in politics, it is still rare.
Angela Merkel once apologized for a useless corona measure.
Robert Habeck , who has developed a certain skill in transforming his own doubts into political capital, speaks of a "learning policy" that includes errors.
But the unwillingness, or even the inability, to account for past mistakes is still part of the habitual inner workings of power.
To regard this as a moral defect on the part of politicians is too short-sighted.
The political attention economy, to which we, the audience, belong, rewards self-critical reflection very little.
We don't really trust anyone who admits mistakes in the future.
Public opinion is an acid bath.
And anyone who has to correct themselves publicly quickly gets the reputation of being incompetent.
In the breathless rhetoric of day-to-day political business, mistakes quickly become disasters, catastrophes - and therefore unforgivable.
Banal admission.
Politicians find themselves in an unpleasant double-bind situation.
They should be sincere and, if you please, self-critical - but if they are, the audience quickly takes offense.
In view of this trap, very clever people like Jens Spahn have invented the advance apology: We will have to forgive ourselves a lot in the end, Spahn announced at the beginning of the pandemic.
In the end, however, this did him no good.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has now admitted that he wrongly held on to the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline for too long.
He was "mistaken" and did not think it possible that Putin "would accept the ruin of his country for his imperial delusions".
This self-awareness sounds somewhat banal.
At present, only the AfD still believes in Nord Stream 2.
There is a consensus in almost the entire EU that no more energy will be bought from Russia as soon as possible.
Persistent error.
Steinmeier's self-criticism therefore only reflects the obvious.
In view of the photos showing him in private with Putin and Foreign Minister Lavrov, she is following a calculation of political expediency.
Self-criticism from politicians is almost always an attempt to open a valve to release pressure from the cauldron.
The Federal President's job also places him above the day-to-day wrangling over power politics.
He doesn't have to fear any list formation or competition from within the party, which will rub his nose in his mistakes, which he himself has admitted, when the opportunity arises.
So is Steinmeier just trying to keep his foot out of the firing line on the cheap, hoping that self-criticism will be an antidote to criticism?
This suspicion is obvious, but premature.
He ignores the fact that anyone who admits to making mistakes is initially standing unprotected in the open and is always taking a risk that is difficult to assess.
Angela Merkel's meagre statement that she stands by her No to Ukraine's accession to NATO in 2008, however, explains nothing.
One sentence, that is an awkward middle ground between silence and justification.
Steinmeier's self-criticism is above all unusual.
Perhaps we, the public, should be more generous with self-criticism.
After all, flawless politicians are an image that hardly anyone believes in, but which is nevertheless extremely tenacious.
On the other hand, we would like to hear more from Steinmeier.
Not only that he was wrong about Putin, but also why this error was so persistent.

After the attacks in El Paso and Dayton: Obama's veiled criticism of Donald Trump

Whatever he would say, it would not be without harsh criticism of his successor Donald Trump.
But that would contradict a long-standing political culture in the USA, which someone like Obama naturally adheres to.

But when the former president does make a statement, as he has now after the mass murders in El Paso and Dayton, the incredible difference in political and moral quality that characterizes the two men immediately becomes clear.

. It is a practical proposal that could be implemented immediately and would have an immediate effect.

Donald Trump keeps adding fuel to the racist fire.
But he also names the intellectual authorship of the racist terror that is spreading in the USA.
It is the radical right-wing websites and networks that incite unstable people to take up arms.
And it is the president himself who keeps adding fuel to the racist fire with his speeches.

Obama doesn't name him, but who should he mean when he writes: "We must firmly reject language that comes from the mouths of our leaders and fuels a climate of fear and hatred or normalizes racial prejudice."

As pleasant as it is to hear such words from a still very influential and popular American politician, the hope that something could change is difficult to maintain in view of the developments of recent years.

He inherited it, if you like, from his predecessor Barack Obama, who already seemed powerless in the face of it.
Four years ago, Barack Obama also denounced the persistent racism.
One of Obama's most moving appearances was a good four years ago, at the memorial service for nine black men murdered by a white supremacist in Charleston.
There, too, he denounced the continuing racism and lax gun laws.
At the end of his speech, however, he sang the church hymn "Amazing Grace", and the predominantly black mourners joined in.
It was a powerful signal not to follow the need for revenge, but to seek forgiveness and reconciliation.
It was a moment of hope that there might be a way out of division and bitterness, hatred and violence in US society after all.
Part of Obama's tragedy is that he has repeatedly succeeded in creating such moments - and yet has been able to translate so little of this spirit into practical policy.
At least he tried.
He is still trying.
Donald Trump doesn't even do that.

Berlin (dpa) - If Germans were allowed to vote in the US presidential election, their vote would be clear: only ten percent would vote for incumbent Donald Trump, while a clear majority of 56 percent would vote for his challenger Joe Biden. 26 percent would not vote for either of them.
This is the result of a survey conducted by the opinion research institute YouGov on behalf of dpa.
According to the survey, supporters of all parties represented in the Bundestag are clearly in favor of Biden - with one exception: among AfD voters, Trump is narrowly ahead with 36 to 35 percent.
SPD supporters are most clearly in favor of Biden (75 to 3 percent), followed by voters of the Greens (72 to 3), the CDU/CSU (71 to 7), the Left (67 to 5) and the FDP (59 to 14).

The answers to the question of who will win the election are not quite so clear. 44% believe that Biden will become the new President of the United States. In contrast, 25% expect Trump to win the election on 3 March.
November will still win despite his deficit in the polls. 31 percent did not provide any information.

As far as sympathy for the two candidates is concerned, a survey conducted by the Bertelsmann Foundation among citizens of all 27 EU member states came to exactly the same conclusion for Germany as YouGov: only ten percent would vote for Trump, 56 percent for Biden.
This means that support for the incumbent president in Germany is still significantly lower than in the European Union as a whole.
Here, Biden is ahead by 45 to 17 percent.
However, it is not preferred in all EU countries.
Poles would vote 38 percent to 30 percent in favor of Trump.

Global investment: Good prospects for British and German stock markets
Political decision-makers around the world have responded to the pandemic with unprecedented consistency and speed.

While high-risk investments such as equities and corporate bonds continue to be supported by massive securities purchase programs and rock-bottom interest rates, the motto for investors is to stay invested now.
We believe that the UK and German equity markets in particular should outperform, even though we expect the general recovery in profits in Europe to lag behind the other regions.
The composition of the UK equity market, which is at a significant discount to other major markets, puts it in a good position to participate in the global recovery following the Covid-19 crisis.
Around 40 percent of the FTSE 100 benchmark group, by market capitalization, consists of value companies, which are valued low in terms of earnings and assets.
In the run-up to the upcoming recovery after the pandemic, several factors also speak in Germany's favor.
The country entered the crisis with solid public finances, with a debt ratio of around 60 percent compared to the eurozone average of almost 85 percent.
As a result, Germany was in a good position to give its economy the extensive stimulus it needed.
Berlin has responded to the crisis with fiscal expansion amounting to around 8 percent of gross domestic product.
If necessary, further liquidity injections can be administered.
The composition of the German market is also proving to be advantageous.
After all, it is strongly characterized by cyclical stocks, which could rise in line with the global economic recovery.
Cyclical sectors such as consumer discretionary, industrials, IT and materials account for more than half of the total weighting of the MSCI Germany.
As a cyclical market, German companies are likely to benefit from an expected economic upturn in key regions such as the EU, the USA and China.
German cyclicals offer the opportunity to bet on a rising purchasing managers' index, an improved economic environment and a recovery in industrial production.
We expect very good earnings growth for 2021 (consensus: around 30%).
The MSCI Germany's dividend yield of 3 percent is also attractive.
In contrast, the US equity rally since March has been narrowly focused on a handful of mega-cap tech stocks.
Last week's massive rotation out of technology stocks weighed on the entire market and highlighted the need for broader diversification.
We recommend investing in long-term trends that are being accelerated by the current crisis.
Supply chains are likely to become less global and more local in the future, which will benefit the automation and robotics sectors.
Europe is home to many of the market leaders in global factory and process automation.

BillerudKorsnäs is a leader in sustainable paper packaging, Süss Microtec shines in chip production and Lotus Bakeries sells six billion caramel cookies: shares, bonds and more for private investment.
The digitalization of the healthcare system is also likely to gain momentum in the wake of the pandemic.
Europe already accounts for 22 percent of the companies in an MSCI index that tracks such "medtech" companies.
Green initiatives, which are at the heart of the EU recovery plan, also offer opportunities for European companies.
In July, the EU heads of state and government agreed on a recovery fund endowed with 750 billion euros, the core elements of which are climate protection and digitalization.
In the long term, areas such as renewable energies, energy efficiency, electric vehicles and infrastructure in connection with mobility and transportation should experience a boost in development.
However, further outbreaks of the virus could lead to the reopening of economies being put on hold.
This would slow down the upswing, but not stop it.
We know more about the virus now than we did at the beginning of the year.

Estimates of both mortality and virus transmission rates are lower than shortly after the outbreak of the pandemic and in some countries a significant proportion of the population has already been infected with the virus.
As a result, policy makers will be able to take measures to contain new outbreaks that are less damaging to the economy, such as mask wearing, contact tracing and social distancing.
There are also indications of progress in the development of vaccines and therapeutics.
While fears of a second wave are causing the strength and pace of the recovery to fluctuate, we expect the economy to gain momentum in the coming year.
All of this suggests that global share prices have further upside potential.
But investors will have to choose particularly carefully.

Close confidant of President Xi elected new head of government in China
With his swearing-in on Saturday, Li succeeded Li Keqiang, the previous prime minister who had been in office since 2013 and was considered a moderate.
However, Li Qiang is overshadowed by the all-powerful President Xi .
He was re-elected by the People's Congress on Friday for a historic third term in office.
He paved the way for this himself when he abolished the previous two-term limit for the president in 2018.
In contrast to most of his predecessors, the new head of government Li, who had risen to number two in the Communist Party in October, had not previously held a high-ranking government office.
However, the 63-year-old has experience at local and regional level.
Li began his career as a worker in a pumping station and steadily worked his way up.

From 2004 to 2007, he worked as Xi's chief of staff when Xi was still party leader in Zhejiang. In 2013, Li became governor of Zhejiang and built up a pro-business reputation. In 2017, Li was appointed Party Secretary of Shanghai - a sign of Xi's great trust in him.
At the beginning of 2022, Li enforced the sometimes chaotic, hard lockdown in the megacity.

As Prime Minister and head of the State Council, Li will now be responsible for day-to-day business, the concrete implementation of Xi's policies and, above all, for economic policy, which the Chinese head of state traditionally leaves to his head of government.

The challenges are immense: last year, China recorded economic growth of just three percent - the last time China's economy grew so slowly was four decades ago, apart from the first year of the pandemic in 2020.
Since the lifting of the strict coronavirus measures, things have been looking up again in China.
But Li must stabilize economic growth, avert a looming financial crisis, support the stumbling real estate market and reassure investors at home and abroad.
His loyalty to Xi is seen by some observers as an obstacle to setting his own priorities in solving these problems.
Li's predecessor, a trained economist, had been thwarted by Xi in his efforts to implement financial reforms.
Hong Kong-based Chinese political expert Willy Lam told the AFP news agency that it is unlikely that Li has the authority to continue on the path of his predecessor.
In addition, Xi believes that stricter control of the economy by the state and the party is necessary - a contrast to the People's Republic's decades-long policy of openness.

Car insurance: Are senior citizens being ripped off?
Individual mobility is still a valuable asset in old age.
As long as their mental and physical health allows, senior citizens naturally do not want to do without their own car.
But this can be expensive: "Car insurers ask senior citizens to pay up," says the comparison portal Verivox.

According to the study, 65-year-old policyholders already pay 16 percent higher premiums compared to drivers ten years younger. 75-year-olds have to pay 65 percent more than their contemporaries who are 20 years younger, and for 85-year-olds, the age surcharge for fully comprehensive insurance is as much as 145 percent compared to policyholders who are 30 years younger, all other things being equal.
The comparison portal refers to model calculations that were carried out using the example of a Mercedes-Benz B 180 or VW Golf VIII 1.0 TSI to be insured.
A case of rip-off and age discrimination?
"There is no reason for us to disadvantage older drivers in any way.
This does not take place in any way," says Karin Benning, spokeswoman for the HUK-Coburg insurance company.
In fact, insurance rates don't just fall out of the sky or are set at will.
Rather, they are the result of complicated calculations that take into account the underwriting risk based on numerous parameters.
Only a few of them are, for example, the place of residence (regional class) or the living situation, the insured vehicle itself (type class) or the mileage.
And the policyholder's years of life.
Increasing risk of accidents.
"The risk of accidents increases with age", explains Verivox Managing Director Wolfgang Schütz, "which is why insurers also charge higher premiums".
In fact, in 2021, drivers over the age of 74 were primarily to blame for the accident in which they were involved in three quarters (75.9 percent) of all cases.
This is according to data from the German road safety organization Deutsche Verkehrswacht.

The Federal Financial Supervisory Authority (BaFin), which is not suspected of taking sides, also speaks of a "demonstrably higher underwriting risk associated with age"; in this respect, it has "no objection" to the practice of insurers charging corresponding surcharges.
The German Insurance Association (GDV) recommends that its member insurance companies demand such an age surcharge from the age of 68.
Many accident-free years.
The good news, however, is that in practice the premium situation for older vehicle owners is often different - and better.
"Anyone who only turns the 'age' setting screw in rate calculators will get an inaccurate picture of the actual insurance premium," says BaFin.
This is because the no-claims bonus class (SF) also plays a major role in the assessment.
And this is where experienced senior citizens often benefit from many accident-free years.
They benefit from the fact that ever higher SF classes are being established.
Whereas just a few years ago only up to 35 claim-free years were recognized, the figure is now 50 years and in some cases even more.
Those who no longer drive to work every day can also point to a lower annual mileage.
This also lowers the insurance premium.
Karin Benning from HUK even notes that "older drivers have the lowest average premiums in our portfolio".
Kathrin Jarosch from GDV, on the other hand, advises "regardless of age" to regularly review your personal life situation and "inform your motor insurer of any changes relevant to your tariff".
In addition to a reduction in mileage, this may involve, for example, a new garage as a protected parking space or the fact that the car is no longer used by other people.
The children can help.
Verivox boss Wolfgang Schütz has another money-saving tip: "Senior citizens can register and insure their vehicle through their adult children".
The 85-year-old B-Class driver would save around 80 percent if his car was registered to his 30-year-old child and he was only registered as the driver.
But this trick may go wrong with the grandchildren.
Apart from their low SF class, very young drivers between the ages of 18 and 25 are still the most accident-prone age group - and therefore also the most expensive.

Fed decision: The Fed must raise interest rates faster

If an extraterrestrial had landed in the USA in recent months, in a country where the key interest rate is zero and inflation is just under eight percent, he would probably have come to the conclusion that the central bankers there are in a deep sleep.
But now they seem to have woken up.

At the meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee on Wednesday, the US monetary authorities, chaired by Jerome Powell, decided to raise the target range for interest rates on the interbank market by 25 basis points to between 0.25 and 0.5 percent.
It was the first interest rate hike in more than three years.
At the beginning of 2020, the Fed pushed the cost of borrowing to almost zero percent due to the coronavirus pandemic.
The economy is now strong enough to manage without the support of ultra-loose monetary policy, Powell said, explaining the interest rate move.
There is an extreme imbalance between supply and demand on the labor market.
Companies are desperately looking for workers, and those willing to work can virtually pick and choose their jobs.
For every unemployed person, there are 1.7 vacancies.
The labor shortage is driving up wages and accelerating inflation.
Even though Powell avoided the term "wage-price spiral" in the press conference, his comments on the labor market were to be seen as an admission that this spiral is already underway.
This threatens to accelerate inflation expectations.
The Fed has therefore raised its inflation forecast for this year (measured by the core rate of the deflator for personal consumption expenditure) from 2.7% to 4.1%.
At the same time, it has reduced its growth forecast from 4.0% to 2.8%, not least due to the war in Ukraine and the ongoing supply bottlenecks.
However, the rate is still well above the figure of 1.8%, which the central bank believes is associated with stress-free economic growth.
So the boom continues.
Powell therefore held out the prospect of further interest rate hikes.
According to estimates by central bankers, the key interest rate is likely to rise to 1.9 percent by the end of this year.
With interest rate hikes of 25 basis points each, this would mean a total of seven interest rate hikes this year, including yesterday's hike.
Four further interest rate hikes are likely to follow next year, bringing the key interest rate to 2.8 percent.
Powell pointed out several times at the press conference that the central bank could certainly raise interest rates more quickly if the situation on the price front so required.
The central bank has made great progress in developing its plan to reduce the balance sheet total, Powell said.
The Fed does not want to replace bonds in its portfolio that are due for redemption by purchasing new bonds.
The method of reducing the balance sheet will be similar to that used by the Fed to reduce its bond holdings after the financial crisis.
However, the balance sheet reduction will take place more quickly this time than back then.
The decision on this will be made at one of the next meetings.
Powell repeatedly emphasized that the Fed would do everything in its power to push inflation back to the target value of two percent.
Price stability is the prerequisite for sustainable economic growth and therefore also for a high level of employment, explained the Fed Chairman.
He is right.
However, the Fed's inflation problem is homemade.

The central bankers around Powell loosened the reins of monetary policy far too much at the start of the pandemic and then let it slide for too long to be able to easily catch up with inflation now with triple steps in interest rates.
The step on the brakes comes late, perhaps too late.
And it is too timid.
Even if the central bankers raise the key interest rate to 1.9% by the end of this year as planned, it will probably remain well below the inflation rate.
The real interest rate therefore remains deep in negative territory and is boosting the economy instead of slowing it down.
The Fed is aiming to raise the key interest rate to 2.8 percent by the end of next year.
This would be above the expected inflation rate of 2.7 percent.
The real interest rate returned to positive territory next year.
But whether the maneuver will succeed is by no means certain.
This is because the Fed's inflation forecast is based on the assumption that base effects will put significant downward pressure on the inflation rate next year.
This is only likely to be the case if prices for energy, food and other goods hardly rise at all in the coming months.
A comparison with the high price indices from this year would then cause the year-on-year growth rates to fall.
