World's best teachers
We Free Democrats are calling for the teaching profession to be strengthened.

This requires attractive working conditions, high-quality training and development, transparent and challenging career opportunities, immaterial appreciation and pay that rewards individual commitment.
We want to develop teacher training nationwide into a dual teacher training program that closely interlinks theoretical and practical phases right from the start.
The shortage of teachers is still omnipresent.
That's why we want to create incentives to get young people excited about the profession again.
Excellent teacher training and professional development
We Free Democrats demand nationwide minimum standards for excellent teacher training.
We need a good balance between academic and pedagogical education.
Digital skills, the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence for learning processes and digital learning and teaching methods must become an integral part of teacher training.
We are also calling for the establishment of a German Teachers' Academy to develop and offer appropriate training courses.
The training courses should be based on the latest scientific findings and regular attendance should be compulsory for teachers.
Immigration and flight
Germany is a country of immigration.
Like all traditional immigration countries, it therefore needs clear rules for immigration according to its own interests, bundled in an immigration code.
At the same time, humanitarian obligations towards those in need of protection must be fulfilled.
We want to combine humanity and order.
We Free Democrats want to create immigration law from a single source in the form of a coherent immigration code.
Making a clear distinction between flight and immigration
For us Free Democrats, the fundamental right to asylum for politically persecuted people is inviolable.
This also includes political persecution on religious grounds or on the basis of sexual identity.
We want to differentiate between politically persecuted people, war refugees and permanent immigrants.
We want to create a separate, unbureaucratic status for refugees fleeing war and civil war - temporary humanitarian protection that is limited to the duration of the war.
This status is to be granted in a straightforward manner once the person's identity has been established, thereby massively reducing the burden on the asylum system.
As a rule, war refugees are supposed to return to their home country once the war is over.
The competencies of the federal and state governments should be clearly separated.

The federal government should be responsible for all issues relating to protection status and the termination of residence, including deportation, so that the federal states can concentrate on the task of integration.
An orderly immigration law also includes the consistent enforcement of the obligation to leave the country through deportation and the creation of
sufficient places in detention pending deportation.

At the same time, particularly vulnerable groups, such as those persecuted on religious grounds or on the basis of sexual identity, need safe procedures and safe accommodation and, in the case of so-called safe countries of origin, special legal advice in order to be able to submit applications in the correct form and on time.
Binding distribution of people seeking protection

As the core of a further development of the Common European Asylum Policy, we Free Democrats call for a binding distribution of asylum seekers among the EU member states, unless they clearly have no prospects of remaining.
If an agreement cannot be reached at EU level in the foreseeable future, Germany should lead the way with like-minded countries.
Countries participating in this
"coalition of the willing" must expect appropriate cuts in funding from the EU budget, which will then be used to finance the costs of taking in refugees.
Preventing secondary migration
We Free Democrats want a fixed, eight-year responsibility of the EU Member State to which a person seeking protection has been assigned.
The transfer back to the responsible EU country must be simplified.
As a rule, those seeking protection should only receive assistance in the responsible EU country.
It must be ensured that this assistance corresponds to a minimum European level in all Member States.
In this way, we want to further develop the Dublin regulations and effectively prevent secondary migration.
Enable asylum applications in embassies of EU member states: Visa on humanitarian grounds
We Free Democrats demand that asylum applications can also be made abroad in the embassies of EU member states.
It must be possible to get to Europe safely - without a life-threatening journey and the risk of falling into the hands of human traffickers.
A visa on humanitarian grounds should also be issued if it is obvious in the individual case that the applicant's life and limb are in immediate, serious and concrete danger.
To this end, clear regulations should be enshrined in European law.
Expand Frontex for external border and sea rescue

We Free Democrats call for a faster expansion of the EU border protection agency Frontex to the planned staffing level of 10,000 officers - accompanied by a structural reform and an expansion of control and transparency mechanisms.
Germany must play a greater role in this.
An area without internal borders requires strong protection of the external borders.
In many cases, the member states can no longer do this on their own.
A strong European border protection agency that supports them in this is therefore in the interests of all Member States and in particular in Germany's interests.
Frontex should also take over sea rescue in order to finally put an end to the cruel deaths in the Mediterranean.
This is a government task.
As long as this is not guaranteed, private bodies that take on this task must not be hindered.
The measures taken with the involvement of Frontex
"Pushbacks", i.e. the illegal pushing back of migrants, must be taken very seriously.
We are committed to the investigation of such incidents and for stricter mechanisms to prevent human rights violations.
This is how we strengthen the European
border protection, improve sea rescue and ensure that human rights are respected at the EU's external borders.
Demanding and promoting integration
We Free Democrats want an integration policy that welcomes diversity and therefore invites immigrants to become part of our society, but also requires them to integrate themselves.
We want to take advantage of the opportunities that immigration offers Germany, because our country is dependent on immigration.
Integration is the key to immigrants becoming part of our society and contributing to its success.

That is why we want to promote integration: through offers to learn our language and our social order, integration mentors based on the Canadian model and additional integration measures aimed specifically at women, children and senior citizens, but also at particularly vulnerable groups.

Bureaucratic hurdles in the immigration and integration process and in taking up employment, such as the priority check or the blocking period for asylum seekers, must be removed and partnerships with countries of origin must be established.
Recruitment strategies are to be developed locally with selected partner countries, for example with language courses and preparatory courses for life in Germany.
For a holistic energy system
We Free Democrats want the energy transition to be more innovative, more open to technology, more international and more holistic.
After all, it's not just about electricity, but also about heating and cooling for buildings, industrial processes and fuels for transportation.
We will not achieve the climate protection targets in Germany by relying solely on direct electrification based on renewable electricity.
Our goal is a cost-efficient, secure and globally networked European energy supply system.
We want a science-based energy policy that focuses on innovation, competition and a high level of social acceptance.
Making energy affordable - abolishing the EEG levy
We Free Democrats want to comprehensively reform the levies, taxes and charges on energy.
This is because Germany currently has the highest electricity prices in Europe for almost all consumer groups.
To this end, we want to reduce the electricity tax to the EU minimum.

We want to gradually abolish the EEG levy (Renewable Energy Sources Act) by financing the funding commitments from the past as far as possible from the revenue from CO2 pricing and by not creating any new funding categories.
Expanding renewable energies in a market economy
We Free Democrats want to make renewable energies fully competitive and end subsidies under the Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG).
We reject legally prescribed expansion paths for individual technologies and state-guaranteed purchase prices.
German electricity customers have already contributed over 200 billion euros to the expansion of renewable energies.
They currently account for around half of electricity generation in Germany and will be able to take on more system responsibility in the future.
A rising CO2 price will make fossil fuels even less attractive and lead to a more demand-driven expansion of renewable energies.
We also want to simplify self-supply with renewable electricity and the market-based use of electricity from old plants that are no longer eligible for the 20-year EEG subsidy.
Secure energy supply - regular stress test
We Free Democrats want regular monitoring (stress test) for security of energy supply and clear criteria for this to be laid down in law.
Because the safe and reliable supply of electricity, heating, cooling and fuel at any time and any place is our priority.
It must not be jeopardized by climate and energy policy measures.
The coal and nuclear phase-out and the increasing feed-in from wind and solar energy, which fluctuates depending on the time and weather, pose enormous challenges for our energy system.
Flexible generation and storage technologies can make an important contribution to overcoming these challenges.
More speed with hydrogen

We Free Democrats want to establish hydrogen and synthetic fuels as the second pillar of the future energy system alongside electricity and drive forward the ramp-up of the hydrogen economy as quickly as possible.
CO2-neutral hydrogen and synthetic fuels can replace fossil fuels in industry, power cars, ships and airplanes or heat buildings.
Volatile electricity from the sun and wind can be stored and transported over long distances by producing hydrogen using electrolysis.

In addition to green hydrogen from renewable energies, we also rely on CO2-neutral "blue" and "turquoise" hydrogen from natural gas for the ramp-up, the production of which allows the carbon it contains to be stored.

The prerequisite for this is that the escape of methane ("methane leakage") during the extraction and transportation of the natural gas for conversion can be ruled out or, where this is not 100 percent possible, compensated for accordingly.
This is the only way we can achieve large quantities at affordable prices in the short term.
In order to ensure the production of energy sources at reasonable costs, investments must be made in plants worldwide.

Photovoltaic or wind power plants at suitable locations in conjunction with connected infrastructure for the production of energy sources that are easy to store and transport can make a major contribution to this.
European Hydrogen Union
We Free Democrats want to promote the establishment of a European Hydrogen Union.

This is because Germany currently imports around 70 percent of its energy requirements and will continue to be dependent on imports of energy sources in the future, despite all efforts on the domestic market.
We must therefore now create a European strategy for the import of climate-neutral gases and fuels.
In addition to the early establishment of international partnerships, part of this strategy must also include the realization of the necessary import infrastructure.
A European Hydrogen Union combines climate protection with a sustainable industry and a secure energy supply.
Hydrogen projects, for example from solar energy at low-cost production sites in southern Europe, can help to reduce economic imbalances within the EU.
For a digital energy transition
We Free Democrats want to accelerate the digitalization of the energy transition in Germany and make it less bureaucratic.
After all, improving energy efficiency, making consumption and tariffs more flexible and ensuring system and supply security can only be achieved through consistent digitalization.
Smart applications can help to drive forward the transition from a centralized to a decentralized energy supply.
We want to simplify the rollout of intelligent metering systems ("smart meters") - as a prerequisite for "smart grids" and for automation through artificial intelligence.
IT and data security must be a cornerstone for protecting this critical infrastructure.
New opportunities and innovations may arise from increasingly data-driven business models.
Digitalization can also leverage enormous energy efficiency potential in the private sector - for example in heat and lighting control and autonomous driving.
Strengthening acceptance of the energy transition
We Free Democrats want to strengthen local acceptance of the energy transition through early public participation, a smart balance with local residents and transparent constitutional procedures.
This is because support for the expansion of renewable energies and grids is generally high and more and more companies want to rely on renewable energies.
For a sustainable energy transition, it is essential that the interests of all stakeholders are taken into account.
In addition to acceptance, this also ensures legal certainty for projects once they have been approved.
Many groundbreaking developments of the past decades would not have been possible without active and forward-looking policies.
Politicians must describe the long lines and the direction and see themselves as drivers of innovation.
It must formulate the key objectives for competitiveness and sustainable employment on which forces should be concentrated.
We need the state as a strategic investor, as a regulatory and creative force to tackle the challenges of our time.
The state and administration must become drivers of innovation and use their buying power.
Public sector investment in key future areas is of central importance.

We will continue the high level of federal investment that we have achieved in this legislative period, with at least 50 billion euros per year, and will also help to ensure that all levels of government participate with a high level of investment.
We will continue to support structurally weak regions through the Joint Task for the Improvement of Regional Economic Structures (GRW).
Local authorities are a key player in the investment process - we must maintain and strengthen their investment power.
Ensuring equal living conditions also means that social services must not be dependent on the financial capacity of the municipality.
To achieve this, we need strong and effective municipalities across the board.
In the course of the coronavirus pandemic, we have already taken further steps to relieve local authorities of social spending.
One necessary step is to relieve the particularly heavily indebted municipalities of one-off high existing debts.
We will also solve the problem of old debts, especially those of East German housing associations.
In Germany, over 300 billion euros are currently spent on public procurement every year.
As a major purchaser of products and services, the public sector in particular must assume responsibility.
We will align public procurement in such a way that it stimulates innovation and serves the goals of socio-ecological change.
To this end, the award criteria should focus more strongly on innovation, collective bargaining, gender equality and climate-friendly sustainability.
Product developments must be able to rely on the state as a consumer.
We need to get better at turning ideas into products and services and promoting start-ups.
We will translate research findings into innovations and investments faster and more broadly.

The Kreditanstalt für Wiederaufbau (KfW) plays an important role here, raising funds on the capital market and, together with the promotional banks of the federal states, channeling them into strategically important sectors of the future, supporting the socio-ecological restructuring of the economy and also promoting start-ups.
We will develop it into a modern innovation and investment agency.
We stand alongside the many companies that take their social, societal and ecological responsibility seriously.
The skilled trades sector is the key partner in making the climate transition a success on the ground.
We will promote the skilled trades by abolishing fees for technician and master craftsman courses and advocating collective bargaining in the skilled trades.
We support the skilled trades in their efforts to counter the shortage of skilled workers with new training concepts and to link vocational training with schools and universities in a practical way.
We promote and recognize the role of the skilled trades in the training and integration of young people from all parts of the world.
Start-up companies are important growth drivers for the economy.
We want to make Germany a leading start-up location in Europe and thus create high-quality jobs in the regions.

In order to encourage more start-ups and enable SMEs to make sensible succession planning, we are focusing on three key points: Organizational support such as one-stop agencies for founders, easier access to capital through project funding as well as public funds for venture capital and a "culture of second chances", including in insolvency law.
We will specifically promote business start-ups by women and in rural areas with our own programs.
We want to support companies for whom the purpose of their economic activity and the long-term existence of their company are more important than short-term profit.
To this end, we will develop a national strategy for the promotion of public welfare-oriented companies and social innovations.
We will improve the legal framework conditions for public welfare-oriented businesses, such as cooperatives, social enterprises, integration enterprises and responsibly owned companies.

Decentralized structures already exist to promote the socio-ecological and digital transformation of our economy - we want to bundle and further develop them into transformation centers as workshops of change that are aimed at established companies as well as social enterprises and non-exit-oriented start-ups, employees, trade unions and civil society.
We will continue to show solidarity with those sectors of the economy that have suffered particular losses during the coronavirus pandemic to the benefit of everyone's health.
This applies to the cultural industry as well as the tourism industry, including the hotel and restaurant sector, which will be different after the pandemic than before.
The focus will be much more on domestic tourism than in the past.
This is an opportunity to make this key economic sector sustainable, climate-conscious and modern.
Germany is one of the safest countries in the world.
We will ensure that this remains the case.
Because anyone who is threatened by crime or feels threatened by it is no longer free to act.
We want to prevent citizens from becoming victims of crime through preventive measures.
Good social, labor market, child, family and integration policies form the necessary basis for successful prevention.
More security in Germany depends on motivated, well-trained and well-equipped police officers.
It is unacceptable that police officers, emergency services and public authority employees are increasingly being attacked and insulted.
They deserve recognition and respect for their work.
This must also be reflected in a modern service law, good working conditions and fair pay for police officers and employees.
As an attractive public service, the federal and state governments must once again become more permeable to each other and at the same time be competitive with industry.
We fight organized crime, especially human trafficking, as well as drug trafficking, gang-related burglaries and white-collar crime.
We make it easier to trace the origin of dirty money.
Continuous and cross-area structural investigations by the state police forces, the federal police and customs together with the BKA and Europol are necessary.
We are improving the structures of the security authorities and ensuring smoother integration with the justice system.
This also requires us to continue the Pact for the Rule of Law.
Proceedings must be initiated immediately if criminal offenses have been committed.
Punishment must be carried out quickly in connection with the crime.
Offenders should serve their sentences in prisons.
They should always be places of social rehabilitation.
Together with the federal states, we will promote measures to protect against radicalization and to deradicalize offenders.
We need to know more about crime trends in order to be able to take more targeted preventive action.
To this end, we will again have the Periodic Safety Report drawn up on a regular basis.

Ukraine wants to reassure creditors with an IMF loan

Securing a new $5 billion loan from the IMF would help reassure Ukraine's other creditors that the war-torn country's macroeconomic situation is under control, President Volodymyr Zelensky's chief economic adviser Oleg Ustenko told Reuters on Friday.

New funding from the International Monetary Fund for about 18 months could serve as the basis for a larger $15 to $20 billion package to help Ukraine deal with the economic crisis caused by Russia's invasion, the adviser said.
He also said Ukrainian officials are in contact with the agency about the possible request, adding that the goal should be to move forward as soon as possible.

Ustenko's comments came weeks after Ukraine's central bank governor, Kirill Shevchenko, told Reuters that he was exploring borrowing up to $20 billion from the IMF over two or three years, an amount that would put Ukraine well above the Fund's "emergency access threshold" for borrowing.
The sheer size of this request had caused heated discussions in the IMF because it would also raise questions about the sustainability of Ukraine's debt.

The revised plan would have been modelled on a financing package agreed in 2015 following Russia's invasion of the Crimea region of Ukraine, which included $17.5 billion in IMF financing but helped leverage a total of $40 billion in financing.

"A $5 billion IMF program would be consistent with previous funding levels and could be a catalyst for funding from other sources, including the EU, the US Treasury and other individual countries," Ustenko told Reuters.

Ukraine, which is having to manage the internal displacement of some 7 million people since Russia's invasion on 24 February, is trying to raise resources to cope with energy shortages, rising inflation and a worsening humanitarian crisis as winter approaches.

The economic contraction reaches 35%-45% in 2022 and the monthly budget deficit reaches $5 billion, while only a third of the roughly $29 billion in aid pledged by the West has been used so far, economists say.

This week, Ukraine's external creditors backed its request for a two-year freeze on payments on nearly $20 billion in international bonds, but Ukraine still has to make $635 million in principal payments on previous IMF loans starting in mid-September.
Ustenko said that Ukraine hopes to move quickly in negotiations with the IMF with the aim of reaching a preliminary agreement before the due date of these payments.

It was a dense chronicle of the upward trajectory of Miramax, and especially its co-founder, Harvey Weinstein, from his first big indie hits in the 90s to the validation of his Hollywood primacy.

From the first publication of the book in 2004 until 2017, the year of the New York Times article that led to his imprisonment, much was suppressed and much was leaked - but few people fell from the clouds when the first accusations were made.
Up to that point, Weinstein had been a sympathetic bastard to some, or an outright bastard to others.
I remember reading the book in shock: This guy is dangerous, I thought, who's going to put him away? Thirteen years after the book, and five years after the scandal broke, now we have a movie.
Maria Shrader's "Someone Spoke" picks up the investigative journalism part of this article, following closely the model set up by Alan J.

Pacula in "All the President's Men": Carrie Mulligan and Zoe Kazan (brilliant - and with great chemistry) play reporters Megan Toye and Jody Cantor who, assigned to investigate sexual assault rumors involving the powerful Miramax mogul, discover a shocking chain of abuse.

Despite the rigid "journalistic" skeleton of the model (which can only be developed "linearly"), Shrader manages to bypass it in a moment that ultimately carries all the dramatic underpinnings of the real story: An audio document, which many of us had heard in those days, is dramatized with still, frozen shots at the scene of the crime, a "composition" that has true cinematic inspiration.
But at the same time, again as the model dictates, nothing here is loud: The film has no extreme tensions and melodramatic crowns.
Only Weinstein's voice stands out, with its angry intensity permeating the sound design of the film.

Is this journalistic coldness responsible for its resounding commercial failure? And I'm not just referring to its opening in Greek cinemas (there's no point in even mentioning the numbers, really) but also to its downfall in America.
People didn't want to meet this story in the cinemas.
Maybe the internet has "killed" the genre.
In a way, it makes sense: the audience that went to see Pacula's film also wanted to be informed - but then it was 1976.
The news now reaches everywhere in seconds.

Not even television can catch up, will cinema catch up? At the same time, major studio films are now exclusively getting wide openings (and whatever we catch on the first weekend), which prevented Someone Spoke from causing a strong run in a few select theaters and "opening" soon after.
This was the rule for every "serious" Hollywood film that was going for the Oscars, as is the case with Shrader's film.
Unfortunately, the new cinematic reality that is taking shape - or at least prevailing these days - dictates other, more inhuman rhythms.
He certainly doesn't produce better films.
Despite its constructional accuracy, "Someone Spoke" is still a film based on evidence that we know, on documents that have been made public.
Maria Schroeder directs with care and wisdom, but since we know what to expect, she could have invested in another narrative, another model.
Except that the "serious" films in Hollywood today are not films about creators, but about "subjects".
The "theme" is now measured by the producers (who have a say in the final product) as something more important than the film itself.

"It would be nice if this trend did not prevail," I would have written if the public had not repeatedly rejected it: Yes, the movie theater model needs to change (it's a long conversation), but movies have also ceased to excite us, to challenge us, to leave us wondering what we saw, to allow us to process it: They are all filmed quickly (because content) and they all have to be "read" quickly (zero ambiguity that is), so that you can see the next one on the lids, so that the market can "run".
As Gloria Swanson said in "Avenue of the West", "It's the pictures that got small".
"Someone Spoke" is a well-written, beautifully performed, and ultimately "warm" film about an important (and meaningful) true story.
Only you leave it the same way you came in.
Ready to see the next one.

19:53 Frontex: 12,407 irregular arrivals in Cyprus in 2022 - 214% increase from last year

The Western Balkans was the most active migration corridor in the first half of 2022, according to preliminary data released by Frontex, the agency responsible for border and coast guard services at the external borders of the European Union.
As reported, in the first six months of the year, a total of around 114,720 irregular entries into the European Union were recorded, having increased by 84% compared to the same period last year.
For the month of June, 23,290 irregular crossings into the EU were recorded, an increase of 59% compared to June last year.
The largest increase was recorded in the Western Balkans corridor, where registrations almost tripled compared to the first half of 2021.
This increase, according to Frontex, can be attributed to the efforts of migrants and asylum seekers already in the region.
In particular, 55,321 irregular crossings were recorded in the Western Balkans corridor between January and June, almost half of all irregular crossings at all EU external borders.
Transits through the Western Balkans corridor mainly include migrants and asylum seekers from Syria, Afghanistan and Turkey.
The Central Mediterranean corridor recorded the second highest number of irregular crossings, with a total of 25,164 in the first half of the year, 23% more than in the same period last year.
In June, 5 651 crossings were recorded in this corridor.
Transits in the Central Mediterranean mainly involve citizens of Bangladesh, Egypt and Tunisia.
In the Eastern Mediterranean corridor, which includes Cyprus, 17,957 arrivals were recorded in the same period, an increase of 125% compared to last year.
In June, 2,220 arrivals were recorded in this corridor.
Most arrivals via the Eastern Mediterranean are citizens of Nigeria, Syria and Congo - Kinshasa (Democratic Republic of Congo).
Arrivals in Cyprus remain an important part of this traffic, as 12,407 irregular arrivals were recorded (an increase of 214% compared to last year).
At the EU's eastern border, 2,452 irregular arrivals were recorded in the first half of 2022 (up 141% year-on-year), mainly by citizens of Ukraine, Iraq and Belarus.
As a reminder, refugees leaving Ukraine through official crossing points at the EU border are not counted as irregular arrivals.
A total of 7.2 million people have crossed into the EU since the start of the Russian invasion, including 6.3 million Ukrainian citizens, according to the latest Frontex data.
Finally, the Communication notes that the number of people attempting to cross the Channel Sea to the UK remains high.
Specifically, 22,400 crossings were recorded in the first half of the year, an increase of 87% compared to last year.

Usage guide... for emojis - They look innocent but they're not, what they really mean (so you don't get confused)
But while the design may look familiar, it may not necessarily look the same when it appears on phones.
The designs you see here are samples designed by Emojipedia for Emoji 15.0.
Companies like Apple, Google and Samsung need to make their own plans for emojis.

The controversial meaning of some emojis.
But how are existing emojis used? For some, they are not what they simply look like.
As it turns out, what they mean to different age groups causes some often very troubling situations and separates Boomers from Millennials and them from Gen Zs.
For example, the ripe peach , apart from the fruit, for most people under 25, is not actually a peach but a nice firm pair of buttocks.
Eggplant, on the other hand, for some people is not just the basic ingredient of a meal, but for some it is a sign of impressive virility or a prediction/invitation to hot sex.
What does the simple smiling face suggest? A lovely, happy thought? For some, no.
Or, at least, not when it implies passive aggression.
Take also as an example, the friendly, smiling, winking wink.
To anyone of an older generation, it could only be something innocent.
We're just sharing a joke or showing that we're joking.
But for a twenty-something, that wink is a sexy, tempting proposition.
All of these, if not used with care, can cause problems in your communication with others and cause you to be misunderstood.

As reported by the Mail on Sunday, according to workplace messaging service Slack, more and more older workers are terrorising their younger colleagues with emojis that are not managed properly, causing embarrassment, to shocked bewilderment and lawsuits.

In a survey of 9,400 office workers around the world, including 1,000 in the UK, Slack found that the most common emoji faux pas in workplaces were images of lips, tongue, a smiling poop and that infamous eggplant.
One might wonder why someone would think it a good idea to send a smiling poop or a pair of big shiny lips to a colleague.
But, to be fair, many of the Baby Boomers surveyed had no idea about these hidden concepts.

Alarmingly, almost half had no idea that eggplant meant anything more than a delightfully bright purple vegetable - while, of course, for almost everyone else it's the most sexually suggestive emoji on the planet.
Speaking to the Mail on Sunday, Olivia Grace, director of Slack, said: "The findings of our research are very clear.
Be careful when communicating with intergenerational emojis... it's good to know that there may be different meanings to avoid any awkward interpretations."
Part of the problem is that emojis are still relatively new.
They originated on Japanese mobile phones in 1997 - the name comes from the Japanese e ("image") + moji ("character") - and have only become popular worldwide in the last decade.

Before emojis, there were emoticons - sideways smiling :) and non-smiling :( - faces made with keyboard characters and invented by Scott Fahlman, a computer science professor at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh who, as Jane Fryer of the Daily Mail speculates, would much rather be remembered for his extensive contributions to computing than for the smiling face he dreamed up one day in September 1982.
Today, however, emojis are everywhere in popular culture.
There are now 3,633 officially recognised emojis and around 10 billion are sent every day.
There's even an annual World Emoji Day (you just missed it, it's on July 17, if you're interested).
In 2015, Oxford Dictionaries declared the emoji "Face with Tears of Joy" as the "word" of the year.
And in 2021, at the height of the Covid pandemic, the syringe emoji was voted the most representative visual image of the year.
Today, emojis are used by everyone from politicians to pop stars and royalty.

Indeed, in their congratulatory Twitter post to Novak Djokovic after his seventh Wimbledon title earlier this month, even the ever-so-formal Duke and Duchess of Cambridge included an appropriate pair of claps and a gold trophy.
There are no hidden meanings there.
Although it's a good thing Kate Middleton and Prince William didn't opt for jazz hands - which, apparently, aren't just jazz hands, but the sign you want to give someone a tight hug.

I want and don't want to lose weight

What I have identified in my thirty years of working with weight disorder is that, often, there is a significant deficit in the weight loss effort, which is one of the most important factors in the non-positive outcome of the weight loss pursuit.
Let's say that this deficit is a verb.
Usually, in trying to lose weight, one uses only the following verbs: "want", "demand", "need" to diet.
However, the problem of obesity, in order not to remain unsolved, needs the verb "to calculate".
A person with a weight disorder needs to be carefully observed by a specialist, but also very carefully by himself.
Even in a simple mathematical problem, you stand, observe the data and start calculating; let alone when the problem is not mathematical but human!
"calculate" is the verb that one necessarily needs to display, to understand its meaning, to appropriate its use, in order to work in its favour.
In "I want to go on a diet" one systematically forgets the "and I don't want to go on a diet" that exists at the same time.
The obese person is in a constant conflict, constantly experiencing the "I want and I don't want to lose weight".
But it is not clear to him that such a thing can happen - "I don't want to lose weight" seems absurd to him; his mind is not working, his logic cannot cope with it!
But it is necessary to realize that the existence of the negative version of the desire itself, i.e. "I don't want to lose weight", is not a matter of logic, it is a matter of emotion.
In "demanding" to lose weight, one systematically forgets the "I cannot bear" to be deprived of the taste and quantity of food, which also exists as an equivalent.
This lack of stamina is experienced as unacceptable.
How is the weakness of resistance demonstrated? But it is the one that sabotages the slimming diet by breaking the rules and undermining the effort.

And finally, in the "must" to diet one forgets the "can't" to diet, which basically means that I don't have the right conditions, I don't organize my diet with diligence, method and system to make it easier for me.
The person with a weight disorder has learned to bypass himself and ends up just being a processor.
That is, to complete the procedures for the resolution or regulation of the problem.
But everything he feels or needs is missing from the dietary arrangement.
Every "want", "demand", "need" to lose weight eliminates a "don't want", "can't bear", "can't" to lose weight.
How it makes them disappear By their simultaneous coexistence.
Cancelled.
There is no progress and no result.
Everything ultimately remains static.
Stagnant and hidden behind the weight of the kilos.
Obesity is an "immobility".
Neither forwards nor backwards.
And if I went forward (lost weight), back again (put on weight).
And if I went back (I got too fat), I make new resolutions to get going again (new diet start).
But in the end I always find myself in the same place.
"Calculating", then, means going down my own paths, which most of the time are unexplored.
"Dieting" for weight loss means I calculate and always find a just reason (excuse) for what I do or don't do.
I justify myself no matter how I diet, either I eat too much and have binge eating or I don't do it properly because I can't or can't stand it.

"Respect" means giving me the space to operate in my own way and my way contains within it my wants, my can'ts, my difficulties, my tiredness, my fears, my understanding, my compassion for myself, my needs.

"Going on a diet" means changing the rules by deciding to get tired to eat the way I should every day, to get tired to find free time because I need to have fun, to push myself to get an hour of my own because I need to relax, to make an effort to get my eight hours of sleep because I need to rest.

It means acquiring data that are unalterable for me that will replace the old rules ("don't eat", "restrain yourself") and the reproaches ("why are you hungry", "you ate again").It means not being mentally pressured.
Because "I sometimes may eat because I'm lonely or because I'm worried"...

Next August, an exhibition entitled "Epidemics - Curse of the past, threat of the future", which will present the most important infectious diseases from ancient times to the present day, will open at the Roman Museum in the city of Hildesheim.
The planning for the exhibition predates the coronavirus pandemic, as it started as early as 2018, when no one could have guessed what would happen globally two years later.
"Our exhibition has become timely," says exhibition curator and historian Oliver Gauert in the empty museum, where daily work continues to prepare the exhibition in a 1,800-square-meter space.
According to the German curator, this is the largest report ever made on epidemics and their impact.
We show human tragedies, but also medical successes
Among other things, visitors can tour a medieval plague hospital and see Paul Ehrlich's (1854-1915) reconstructed laboratory where he made salvarsan, the first treatment for the scourge of syphilis.

"We show the pain and human tragedies caused by epidemics to humanity, but also the successes of medical science," says Oliver Gower, who secured the cooperation of many experts and institutions for the exhibition.
These include the Heimholtz Institute for Epidemiological Research in Braunschweig, the Paul Ehrlich Institute and the Hanover Medical School.

"The aim of the exhibition is to show the public the impact that epidemics have had on the evolution of the human species, be it the plague during the early Middle Ages or tuberculosis in modern history," says pulmonologist and epidemic researcher Tobias Velte, who heads the expert advisory committee.
According to the German doctor, "there will always be viruses.
Our main goal is not to wipe them off the face of the earth, but to learn to live with them."
Epidemics have sometimes benefited populations.

At a time when for doctors and infectious disease specialists the risk of a pandemic was always a real possibility, most people were surprised by the scale of the coronavirus pandemic, with 111 million cases and an estimated 2.5 million victims worldwide.

"Especially in the Western world there were many who believed that because of better hygiene, vaccines and antibiotics, epidemics were once and for all a thing of the past," says historian Oliver Gower, adding: "But sadly in other parts of the world the deaths didn't stop, whether we're talking about AIDS, malaria or the Ebola virus.
The report shows, for example, that even today leprosy is still marginalised and stigmatised in many parts of the world.
Pandemic conditions permitting, the exhibition will close its doors at the end of March 2022 and then travel to other German cities.
It is perhaps comforting that epidemics have in many cases brought about important social changes that have benefited populations.

For example: After the last cholera epidemic in 1892 in Germany, the city of Hamburg built a new waterworks and a waste incineration plant, while the authorities took measures to make living conditions more hygienic for citizens.
As far as the coronavirus pandemic is concerned, we can already see that the crisis has accelerated the process of digitalisation in many areas of our lives.

It is in Revithoussa and the new floating storage tank (FSU), and not in Italy, that the strategic gas reserves that under the EU's plan Greece will have to maintain for the coming winter will finally be installed.

In the absence of an available underground storage facility, Greece is obliged under the European plan for security of gas supply to maintain reserves of 15% of its total consumption in another European country.
The installation of the new FSU in Revithoussa enabled the country to avoid the high cost of storing stocks in Italy and to ensure their immediate availability in case of emergency.

Thus, RAE amended, after the consultation, the original Preventive Action Plan for security of supply and proposes to operate the new floating storage facility of Revithoussa as a place for the maintenance of security stocks.
The new floating tank has enabled the country to avoid the high cost of storing reserves in Italy.

The obligation concerns power plants without the possibility of operating with an alternative fuel to natural gas and for quantities of 0.57 terawatt-hours for a period of five months, namely from 1 November 2022 to March 2023.
The plan also provides for the possibility of using the stocks during the five-month storage period, provided that the quantities are replenished no later than 14 days after stocks have been halved.
Producers operating this category of gas plants will have to submit a security reserve supplier declaration to DESFA by 1 October 2022 at the latest.

In Italy or in another EU country of their choice, provided that the storage and transportation costs are not higher than in Italy, or if they prove that there is no availability in the neighbouring country, importers will have to store commercial gas stocks totalling 1.14 TWh for the same period.

The quantities were calculated on the basis of the maximum technical possibility of importing natural gas at the entry point of Nea Mesimbria where the Azeri gas enters the system via TAP, since the LNG stored in Italy will reach the Greek system through a virtual reverse flow.

These costs will be compensated, like the capital costs of maintaining reserves, by the security of supply fee recovered from gas consumers.
The cost of supply is borne exclusively by the companies and at today's prices is around €220 per megawatt hour.

Updated Pfizer/BioNTech and Moderna's updated twin-twin mRNA booster vaccines against Covid-19 provide increased additional protection against the new coronavirus subtypes in people who had two to four doses of the older vaccines, the CDC says.

Pfizer/BioNTech and Moderna's updated twin-twin mRNA booster vaccines against Covid-19 provide increased additional protection against the new coronavirus subtypes in people who have had two to four doses of the older vaccines.

This is shown in a new study by scientists at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) , the first to evaluate the effectiveness of updated vaccines based on real-world evidence rather than laboratory data.

The findings, published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, confirm the initial results of laboratory studies by the vaccine companies themselves, which had shown that the updated twin vaccines after one month lead to the production of more antibodies against the BA.4/BA.5 subvariants of the Omicron variant than the original single vaccines.
The study involved more than 360,000 people.
It compared the booster updated twin vaccines (targeting both the original coronavirus and Omicron's newer BA.4 and BA.5 sub-variants) with the original vaccines from the same companies.
The study found that people aged 18-49 years have the greatest benefit from the updated vaccines compared to older people.

Specifically, according to Reuters, when the updated Covid-19 twin-dose vaccine is administered eight or more months after the previous dose, its relative additional efficacy - compared to that of the original vaccine in terms of preventing symptomatic disease - is 56% in people aged 18-49 years, 48% in people aged 50-64 years and 43% in people aged 65 and over.
Improved efficacy drops to 28% to 31% when booster doses are given only two to three months after the previous vaccination.
So far in the US only 35 million people or about 10% of the population have received the updated twin vaccines.

The researchers stressed that everyone should get these booster vaccines, but acknowledged that these vaccines may not be as effective in the future, as variants of the coronavirus continue to evolve.
Indicatively, in the last two months, the BQ.1 and BQ.1.1 sub-variants tend to dominate in the US, overtaking the BA.5.

Future eurozone bailout programmes should be aimed more at restoring economic growth rather than focusing mainly on fiscal tightening and their duration should be determined accordingly, an independent report commissioned by the European Stability Mechanism (ESM) says, according to a Reuters report.

Greece lost access to markets in 2010, as it emerged that the 2009 budget deficit was 15.4% of GDP instead of the 3.7% deficit forecast earlier.
Athens has had to rely on cheap loans from Eurozone countries for almost nine years to meet its financing needs.

Two American universities collaborated with the ICCT on this research.

Significant increase in cases of patients with cardiomyopathy due to stress or cardiomyopathy
Tacochubo or "broken heart syndrome" was documented by a new US scientific study during the Covid-19 pandemic.
This syndrome occurs after physical or mental stress and causes dysfunction or failure in the heart muscle.
The cause of this cardiomyopathy is thought to be the production of increased stress hormones, which temporarily reduce the heart's ability to beat normally.
Patients usually have symptoms similar to a heart attack, such as chest pain and shortness of breath, but do not have blocked coronary arteries.
Other symptoms may include cardiac arrhythmia, fainting, low blood pressure and cardiogenic shock (inability of the heart to pump enough blood to meet the body's needs).

The researchers, led by cardiologist Ankur Kalra of the Cleveland Clinic, who published the paper in the American medical journal JAMA Network Open, found a large increase in the proportion of cardiac patients with such a syndrome during the pandemic (7.8%) compared with the period before the onset of Covid-19 (only 1.7%).
Also, patients with a 'broken' heart stayed in hospital longer in the pandemic than in the pre-pandemic period.
However, there was no significant difference in the mortality of patients with stress-related cardiomyopathy before and after the pandemic.
Also, this syndrome did not seem to increase the likelihood of infection, as all patients tested negative for coronavirus.
"The Covid-19 pandemic has caused multiple levels of stress in the lives of people around the world.
People are not only worried about themselves or their families getting sick, but also about financial and emotional issues, social problems and possibly loneliness and isolation.
Stress can have physical effects on our bodies and hearts, as shown by the increased number of stress-related cardiomyopathy diagnoses we see around us," said Dr. Calra.
Usually, patients with such cardiomyopathy recover in a few days or weeks, although sometimes the disorder can cause more serious damage to the heart or brain, which can rarely be fatal.
Typically, this syndrome is treated with medications that lower blood pressure and slow down the heart rate.

How do electric cars recover energy?
The answers to this fundamental question for engineers and drivers alike vary, depending on the manufacturer and model.
Some electric vehicles always recover energy during any drive phase.

In the case of its all-new electric models, ID.3 and ID.4, Volkswagen has chosen a different, more effective strategy: free trolling takes priority because any energy conversion inevitably leads to losses.
This applies to the D (Drive) position, the car's main function, which is automatically activated at every start.
Free-rolling mode, in which the driver lifts his foot off the accelerator pedal early, makes driving relaxed and predictable.
If the driver wants to slow down further, he or she presses the brake pedal to activate brake energy recovery.

For up to about 0.25 g, in other words, for the majority of everyday braking actions, it is the electric motor that performs the braking, while the electric servo brake activates the mechanical wheel brakes only in situations requiring greater deceleration.
The transition from engine braking to hydraulic braking is almost imperceptible, thanks to the extremely precise and fast control of the drive and braking systems.
These systems also ensure that the rear wheels, where brake energy recovery takes place, always have sufficient traction.
Every model in the ID. family has Eco Assistance predictive support as standard.
This analyses data from the car's navigation system and sensors and provides the driver with effective support for efficient and relaxed driving.

As soon as ID.3 or ID.4 approaches a zone that requires slow speeds - such as residential areas, intersections or bends - Eco Assistance alerts the driver to lift his or her foot off the accelerator pedal.

The most high-energy light ever observed has been detected on Earth
Chinese and Japanese astrophysicists have announced that they have detected over Tibet the highest energy photons ever seen coming to Earth from the universe.

These are gamma rays with energies of up to 450 trillion electronvolts (TeV), originating from the spectacular Crab Nebula, the remnant of a stellar explosion observed by Chinese astronomers almost 1 000 years ago.
Today at the heart of this beautiful nebula, at a distance of about 6 523 light years from Earth, is a powerful and very dense neutron star (pulsar), which is thought to emit very high-energy light.

The 90 researchers of the ASgamma experiment in Tibet, who published the paper in the physics journal Physical Review Letters, according to Science, announced that between 2014-2017 they detected 24 gamma rays with energies of 100 to 450 TeV.
The previous record holder was 75 TeV gamma rays detected by the High Energy Gamma Ray Astronomy experiment in the Spanish Canary Islands.
By comparison, the photons from our Sun that reach our planet have an energy of only a few electronvolts.
The ASgamma experiment has nearly 600 gamma-ray detectors, which convert the impact of a particle into an electronic signal.
The detectors, in underground water tanks, are spread over a vast 66,000 square metre area in a Tibetan valley at an altitude of 4,300 metres.
When the gamma rays hit the Earth's atmosphere, they create a "rain" of subatomic particles, which fall on the detectors, which in turn record their energy and source.
A key difficulty is to distinguish between gamma rays and cosmic rays, i.e. charged particles that also reach high energies and cause corresponding "showers" of particles on Earth.
Fortunately, in the second case, fewer muons ("cousins" of electrons) are created than are caused by gamma rays.
The detection of muons allows the separation between gamma rays and other cosmic rays.
Gamma rays travel in straight lines and locating their source in the universe is easier than for cosmic rays, which are affected by intervening magnetic fields and do not follow straight paths.
Physicists estimate that the magnetic field of a pulsar accelerates electrons to energies much higher than those achieved by accelerators on Earth.

These electrons then collide with low-energy photons (the cosmic background radiation that pervades the universe) and shoot them out at much higher energies now to the far reaches of the galaxy, reaching the Earth.
According to the researchers, the Crab Nebula is now considered the most powerful physical accelerator known in our galaxy.
Apart from neutron stars, the huge black holes at the centre of galaxies are thought to be another source of very high-energy photons (gamma rays).
New, more powerful observatories in the future, such as the under-development Cherenkov Telescope, may detect even stronger radiation from a source in the universe.

A new, much shorter and less expensive way to treat cancer patients with radiation opens a new, much shorter and less expensive way to treat cancer patients with radiation, according to pioneering research by scientists in the US, led by an oncologist of Greek origin.

The new FLASH radiotherapy-express has begun to be developed at the Abramson Cancer Center of the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine and the researchers, led by Professor of Oncology Konstantinos Koumenis, after relevant experiments on animals (rodents), published the relevant paper in the International Journal of Research Oncology, Biology & Physics.

K. Koumenis is a graduate of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki (1989), with a PhD from the University of Houston, Texas (1994), while the research team includes Ioannis Verginadis and Anastasia Velalopoulou.
What the first tests showed.
Scientists used proton radiation to create a 100 to 200 millisecond dose in an accelerator (cyclotron) that - in theory at least - is enough to give a cancer patient all the radiotherapy they need.
The first trials of the FLASH technique show that it has the same effect on tumours as traditional photon therapy, without damaging healthy tissue due to its very short duration.

Other scientific teams have created similar dose-expressions but using low-energy electrons, which do not penetrate deep enough into the body (only five to six centimetres) to have the same therapeutic utility for internal tumours.

The new technique (Proton FLASH Radiation Therapy System), tested at the Roberts University Proton Therapy Centre, shows that, with appropriate technical modifications, current proton accelerators can achieve doses of clinical utility.
Clinical trial in humans.
Researchers are already preparing for their first clinical trial in humans.
At present, the FLASH technique has only shown its effectiveness in small animals and small tissue areas.
The method needs to be improved to be proven to have a similar effect over a larger area of the body and on larger bodies such as the human body.
Furthermore, the dose will aim to last less than 100 milliseconds.
Remarkably, scientists have yet to understand exactly how proton bombardment radiotherapy works and, more importantly, how it manages to avoid damaging nearby healthy tissue.
It is not clear why cancer cells react differently from healthy cells to treatment, with the result that the former are destroyed but the latter remain intact.

Scientists estimate that proton or high-energy electron-express radiotherapy will be clinically available in five to ten years, even for tumours that are currently difficult to treat with radiotherapy.

The Commission proposes a cap on the price of FA at €275 per megawatt hour

A market correction mechanism to protect EU businesses and households from episodes of excessively high gas prices in the EU was announced by the Commission in response to the ongoing energy crisis, according to a statement.

The European Commission is proposing to cap the price of gas at €275 per megawatt hour for next month's TTF contracts, Energy Commissioner Countrywoman Simpson announced at a press conference in Brussels today.
This mechanism complements measures to reduce gas demand and ensure security of supply through diversification of energy supply.
The new mechanism aims to reduce volatility in European gas markets while ensuring security of gas supply.

Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the rigging of energy supplies, gas prices have seen unprecedented price spikes across the EU, reaching historic highs in the second half of August this year.
The extreme price rises for almost two weeks in August were extremely damaging to the European economy, with contagion effects on electricity prices and an increase in overall inflation.
The Commission proposes to prevent the recurrence of such episodes with a temporary and well-targeted instrument of automatic intervention in the gas markets in case of extreme gas price increases.
Security ceiling on gas prices.
The proposed instrument consists of a security price cap of EUR 275 for TTF derivatives for the following month.
The Transmission Transfer Facility (TTF), which is the most commonly used benchmark for the price of gas in the EU, plays a key role in the European wholesale gas market.
The mechanism will be automatically activated when both of the following conditions are met: The TTF export settlement price of the preliminary month exceeds €275 for two weeks.
TTF prices are 58 euros higher than the benchmark LNG price for 10 consecutive trading days within the two weeks.

When these conditions are met, the Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER) will immediately publish a market correction notice in the Official Journal of the European Union and inform the Commission, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) and the European Central Bank (ECB).
The following day, the price correction mechanism will come into effect and orders for pre-month TTF derivatives that exceed the safety price cap will not be accepted.
The mechanism can be activated from 1 January 2023.
Safeguards to ensure security of supply and market stability.
The proposed Council Regulation includes safeguards to avoid disruptions in energy and financial markets.

In order to avoid security of supply problems, the price cap is limited to a single forward product (TTF forward products), so that market players are still able to meet demand requests and supply gas on the spot and OTC market.

To ensure that gas demand does not increase, the proposal requires Member States to notify within two weeks of the activation of the market correction mechanism the measures they have taken to reduce gas and electricity consumption.

Once today's proposal for a market correction mechanism is adopted in the Council, the Commission will also propose to declare an EU alert under the Save Gas for a Safe Winter Regulation adopted in July, triggering mandatory gas savings to ensure demand reduction.

In addition, there will be continuous monitoring by ESMA, the ECB, the Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER), the Gas Coordination Group and the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSO-G).
To react to possible undesirable negative effects of the price limit, the proposal provides that the mechanism can be suspended immediately at any time.

This can happen: Automatically, by deactivation, when its operation is no longer justified by the gas market situation, i.e. when the gap between the TTF price and the LNG price is no longer covered for 10 consecutive trading days.
By a Commission suspension decision, where risks to the security of supply of the Union, to demand reduction efforts, to gas flows within the EU or to financial stability are identified.
There is also the possibility for the Commission to prevent the triggering of the mechanism if the competent authorities, including the ECB, warn that such risks are realised.

France has been facing a heat wave for a week now that has caused major fires in the south-west of the country.

In 1911, the French of La Belle Epoque experienced a heatwave that was as deadly as it was unusual.
Coming straight from the USA, the "dome of fire" hit Europe, especially the Netherlands, Belgium and especially France.
For 70 days, from 4 July to 13 September, the heat in France was stifling.
Very high temperatures, combined with high levels of solar radiation and a complete absence of rain, the heat wave engulfed the entire country.
After a relative lull at the end of August, it returned in September and only stopped in the middle of the month.
Over 46,000 dead, of which 30,000 were babies.

"In 1911, the people of France experienced more than two months of extreme drought and high temperatures," recalls Catherine Rollet, author of a book dedicated to analysing the demographic, medical and political consequences of this phenomenon.
("The Heat Wave of 1911: Demographic and Medical Observations and Political Reactions").
It was a significant rise in temperatures, which affected the whole country, but even worse in northern France, adds Patrick Silberman, professor emeritus of health history, quoted by Ouest-France.
Temperatures quickly reached 36°C and sometimes exceeded 40°C.
On 22 and 23 July 1911, 38 °C were recorded in Lyon, Bordeaux and Châteaudun.
In August, in Paris, temperatures exceeded 30°C for 14 consecutive days.
Temperatures were 5 to 7.5 degrees Celsius above normal.
In 1911, the country faced a heat wave, but also an epidemic of "green diarrhoea" (green stools due to bacterial infection) that wreaked havoc on very young children, the teacher recalls.
The heatwave quickly affected all strata of society.

A total of 46,719 people died during this period from extreme heat, and among these victims were 30,000 babies under one year old, representing half of the total number of children who died in 1911, says Patrick Silberman.

Poverty and heat, a deadly combination.
These staggering numbers have several explanations, according to the health history professor.
At that time, the excessive heat was conducive to microbial contamination of drinking water.
In 1911, there were no chemicals or facilities needed to preserve and protect the water.
The heat favoured the appearance of flies, which carried all kinds of bacteria.
Moreover, at the beginning of the century, transport was mainly carried by animals such as horses, donkeys and mules.

For some decades, political scientists have taken two unchanging principles for granted: that ultimately, voters' attitudes are determined by how their choices affect their pocketbooks, and that the winner is whoever manages to win the middle ground.
But lately, things have been happening all over the world that are forcing us to reconsider this doctrine.
What's this about? I think the case of Brexit is proving illuminating.
The party that favoured remaining in the European Union put the emphasis exclusively on the dire economic consequences of exit.
And he lost.

The explanation is that this ominous prediction of the economic consequences, accurate or inaccurate, took a back seat because for most of those who chose Brexit, the dimension that interested them was another: how the English (unlike the Scots and the Northern Irish for reasons beyond the present) would regain full national sovereignty.
Part of which, according to Brexit supporters, had either been ceded to Brussels or was in danger due to the influx of migrants from other EU countries.
To put it another way, the warning/threat of what would happen to the economy and thus to the pockets of the British people was empty - like scaring an atheist that he will go to Hell.
This was clearly seen in the election period.

The evidence presented by the pundits was not answered in the same specific way but was dismissed as a "scare campaign" launched by the establishment, while any assurance from the leaders of Brexit, i.e. the Far Right of the Conservatives, that "everything will be fine, don't listen to them" was immediately accepted as absolute and absolute truth.
Because that's simply what they wanted to hear.
Even today, as predictions are beginning to come true, polls show only a slight decline in Brexit supporters.

The initial complacency about the coming economic hardship has given way to a tougher and at the same time more honest attitude: Yes, we will suffer at first, but it will be worth it if we are to rid our country of the uncontrolled presence of foreigners.

I am not saying that people do not care about their pockets; but there is growing evidence that the problem of identity, i.e. who we are, marginal if not unthinkable until recently in developed countries, is emerging as the question that determines political choices.
This shift also explains the refutation of the other firm principle that elections are decided by who wins the centre.
Because the question "Who are we?" is not open to compromise and sober calculations of loss and gain.
It often even transcends the ideological differences between Conservatives and Labour.
It is an existential issue and it works in many ways because it echoes a series of disparate, accumulated and diffuse insecurities.
"Take back control" was the motto of Brexit.
Going back to when phones were something we could all handle, back when you bought a ticket at the counter and not online.
Back when transactions were done face to face and not by e-mail.
Back when children respected their parents.
Back when men were men and women were women.
For some, that's when the sun never set on the British Empire.
And for others, back when anyone born a miner died a miner.
In a world that is changing at an unprecedented speed, slow movers feel that the young and those who have been able to modernise have abandoned them.

So when a referendum gives them the opportunity to register their desperation, they will follow not the cool and calm but the most extreme demagogues - Farage in Britain and Trump in the United States.
They are not "tamed" by power like Ronald Reagan, because their stay in power is only ensured by the constant reproduction of the extreme discourse that gave them it.
There are many messages to the left and it would be a colossal mistake to close our ears.
Until now, the principle has been that those who resented were, even potentially, "ours".
A look around us today proves otherwise.
Those who feel wronged, neglected, are today seeking the salvation and revenge promised by the Far Right.
In Greece, for various historical reasons, the role of saviour and avenger was assumed by SYRIZA, adopting any demand that embarrassed the governments of the time.
Electorally and in the short term it has paid off.
But it does not bode well for the future.

European democracy at risk?

Nationalism in all European countries, fuelled by at least two main causes, the fear of immigrants and economic inequalities, which intensified during the crisis, has appeared threatening to European democracy, as the suffering it led to a few decades ago has been forgotten.

The least economically and socially advantaged citizens of almost all European countries feel insecure in the face of the spectre of unemployment, which they consider to be caused by the migratory flow, and of course by the new technological revolution.

As the traditional political parties, conservative and/or social democratic, do not seem to be able to provide convincing answers to their concerns, these citizens are looking for other, unfortunately dead-end, solutions.

This situation is exacerbated by the nationalist political and antisystemic forces that claim that the main culprit is the European Union, which supposedly prevents the implementation of national policies that would "miraculously" solve all the problems.

These anti-systemic political forces, anti-European and anti-democratic, also blame liberal parliamentary democracy as responsible both for the tolerance of immigrants and for the widening of economic and social inequalities in Western and Eastern Europe in different forms in each country.

These forces, taking advantage of the way the EU has dealt with the refugee issue and the economic crisis through fiscal discipline and the reduction of workers' salaries, as well as the current restrictive economic policy, due to European rules, are seeking a dead-end return to the nation-state in order to "avoid European subordination".

Both the supporters of Brexit in Britain and the political forces currently in power in Italy, the Party of Alternative in Germany, the National Front and the anti-government movement, which are trying to appropriate extreme political elements in France, the anti-European political forces in the governments of Hungary and Poland, etc. have certain characteristics in common, insofar as they are inspired by nationalist, anti-democratic and anti-European ideas.

On 22 January 2019, a new Franco-German Treaty was signed, as a continuation of the 1963 Treaty of Elysée, with the declared aim of contributing to the expansion of cooperation between the two countries in all areas and through this to the construction of a united, sovereign and democratic Europe.
This fact has gone almost unnoticed in our country, as it is busy with its own problems in an electoral and divisive atmosphere.

This new Franco-German Treaty, between two Governments with a firm commitment to European Integration and Liberal Democracy, because it is concluded by the two largest countries of the EU, which were and are the pillars of the European construction, has a significant pan-European contribution to the consolidation of these principles and is of interest to all European countries and of course to our country.

Despite the fact that both leaders are in difficulty, with Chancellor Merkel leaving power and President Macron facing social controversy at home, the Agreement is a very important European event, even if in our country it was not appreciated in all its dimensions.

Moreover, the confrontation between the supporters of European integration and liberal democracy on the one hand with Macron and Merkel and the anti-European and nationalist forces with Salvini, Le Pen and Orban has begun.
The arguments of the former must convince European citizens of the value of democracy and European integration in a worrying international environment where authoritarianism is everywhere.
For this reason, this agreement is of great interest, as it comes at a crucial phase of the European course close to the upcoming European elections in May 2019.

Population decrease by 414,000 in the years 2011-2019

On July 10, the Statistical Office of the European Union (Eurostat) released data on the population of the EU member states and the United Kingdom on 1.1.2020 as well as on births and deaths in these states in 2019.

Based on these data and the corresponding data of the same service for the population on 1.1. of the years 2011-2019 and the births and deaths in the years 2011-2018, we examine in this article the evolution of the population of our country in the period 2011-2020.
Before we proceed, we should note that since the end of World War II the population of the country has been growing continuously until 1.1.2013, the year in which it reached its highest level.
This increase is due on the one hand to the natural change in population (births minus deaths) and on the other hand to the net inflow or outflow of population (inflow minus outflow).

Unfortunately, the natural increase of the population due to a decrease in births and increase in deaths turned into a natural decrease in the six years 1998-2002 and recovered thanks to the births of foreigners in the years 2004-2010.
From 1990 to 2010, population growth was mainly due to net population inflow.
But since 2011, the country's population has been declining and continues to do so.
This evolution and the factors behind it are shown in the Table.
This table shows that in the period 2011-2019: The population of the country (at different rates) was continuously decreasing.
The total decrease during this period amounted to 413,692 and was due on the one hand to the predominance of deaths over births by 226,549 and to the net outflow of population by 187,143.
The predominance of deaths over births was continuous (at different rates because of the different rates of change in births and deaths).
More specifically, in the five-year period 2011-2015, deaths exceeded births by an average of 17,900 per year, while in the four-year period 2016-2019 by 34,250.

The net population outflow of 187,143 is due on the one hand to the net outflow (new immigration) of 265,400 in the five-year period 2011-2015 and the net population inflow of 62,900 in the four-year period 2016-2019, which mitigated the population decline due to the large natural decline.

Defence Expenditure.
Defence spending has fallen during the memorandum years, due to the decline in GDP and cuts.

They now amount to $5.5 billion in 2019 or about 2.6% of GDP, when in the 2000s they exceeded $7 billion and in 2009 they peaked at $10.6 billion in current values and 3.2% of GDP, according to SIPRI data.
At the same time, Turkey's defence spending in 2000 was $16 billion or 2.5% of GDP, while in 2019 it was $20.4 billion or 2.7%.
Both countries are obliged, because of NATO membership, to a minimum expenditure of 2% of GDP.
The other thing to note is that these are total costs, i.e. including salaries, pensions, operating costs and equipment.
The latter in the case of Greece amount to 12.3% of total spending in 2019, while in Turkey it is 38.6%, with a 20% share indicated by NATO.
Therefore, not only has our country's total defence spending been reduced, but this has been at the expense of the armament part of it.
Based on the 2021 Budget, spending on armaments amounted to €515 million in 2020, €258 million in 2019 and €320 million in 2018!

The increase for 2021 to €2.5 billion is de facto imperative, but we believe that it essentially responds to underinvestment in previous years, i.e. it covers programs that were left behind (F16 upgrade, submarine and Mirage equipment, missile launcher completion), as well as part of future planning.
The major factor that affected spending is the decline in GDP during the memorandum years.
More specifically, in 2000, Greece's GDP was about $130 billion, the same as Israel's, while Turkey's was $270 billion.
In 2018, Greece's GDP was $203 billion, Israel's was $379 billion, while Turkey's had grown to $771 billion.
That is, the GDP ratio of Greece-Turkey from 1:2 in 2000 has become almost 1:4!
This shows that economic independence and economic stability affect national security.
They are interconnected, as is the EEZ and its deposits, which may be worth more than the country's debt, if we look at it from the economic point of view.

Here are the 662 zones in Paris where scooters will be slowed down from Monday.
Town hall forecourts, shopping streets, gardens...
Starting this Monday, November 15, electric scooters from Dott, Lime and Tier, the three Paris-based operators, will be automatically restricted to a maximum speed of 10 km/h in 662 zones.
This system, which the JDD reveals, is being put in place after a test phase launched on June 28 in some 15 areas of central Paris, notably the Nelson Mandela garden near Les Halles.
"It's a joint project involving the operators, Paris City Hall and the local authorities, who helped us identify the zones," explains Sylvain Martin, Managing Director of Tier Mobility in France.
The restriction will apply to all users of free-access scooters.
Since the beginnings of free floating, just three years ago, the framework has continued to evolve.
A necessity in the face of the chaos caused by the thousands of scooters of the 11 operators present in April 2019.
The Mobility Orientation Act (LOM) of December of the same year introduced a new system of prior authorization for self-service two-wheelers.
Paris City Hall has taken advantage of this to clean up its act.
Gone are the 11 rental companies.
Since September 2020, only three of them - Dott, Lime and Tier - have been allowed to operate a maximum of 5,000 scooters each for a fee of 65 euros per device and for two years.
Parking spaces have also been created and certain areas, such as parks, have already been excluded.
So this new limitation could annoy users, who will see their journey times lengthen.
But it's nothing to be afraid of," says Nicolas Gorse, General Manager of Dott France.
As with Les Halles, these are heavily pedestrianized areas.
It's therefore only natural to reduce speed in order to avoid accidents and allow the different road users to live together peacefully."
However, Sacha, a young engineering school graduate and daily user of one of the services, is not convinced by this argument. "10 km/h is very slow.
I'm waiting to see if the zones are close together," he grumbles.
If that's the case, I'll buy one."
Private scooters are not subject to this automatic restriction.

So do these 662 zones appear to be an injustice and a brake on development for the three operators?
No," says Antoine Bluy, Managing Director of Lime in France.
This regulation suits us fine.
In fact, it's indispensable.
We have a duty to set an example so that scooters are accepted in the long term."
