Aman and Netanyahu do not see eye to eye on the Iranian threat
In a previous post I pointed out that the alarmist talk about a "quick breakthrough" for the first bomb, relies on an abstract theoretical analysis to measure time.
This is not an objective scientific calculation that heralds an immediate concrete threat.

"Breakthrough time" is the time required, subject to a number of preliminary assumptions, to produce enough enriched uranium at a high military grade (90%) for a first bomb, if and when Iran decides to build one.
The main failure in the quantity scenarios for a rapid breakout, stems from the fact that they rely on the enrichment of uranium at the civilian nuclear sites in Iran.

The Islamic Republic's civilian nuclear program is under the most intrusive monitoring regime in nuclear history: continuous monitoring based on daily visits by IAEA inspectors and real-time data transmissions to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) headquarters in Vienna.
Also, and based on the "Additional Protocol" of the IAEA, inspections are held at short notice at undeclared sites.

In this situation, Iran will have difficulty diverting uranium enriched to a low civilian grade - which is allowed to it according to the nuclear agreement and in accordance with its membership in the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) - to enriched uranium to a prohibited military grade.
The whole reason for the existence of the IAEA is to warn against such deviation.

Therefore, 1,300 kg of civilian low-grade enriched uranium under the supervision of the IAEA at the end of 2020 does not necessarily mean a fast straight line for military enrichment for the purpose of obtaining fissile material for a bomb.
Moreover, in order to quickly break through and obtain enriched uranium of a high military grade, Iran will have to expel the IAEA inspectors from its territory and withdraw from the NPT treaty.
These two necessary steps were taken by North Korea at the time in order to develop its nuclear weapons.
From the reflection of AMN's assessment in the media reports (as mentioned, no authorized text was published) it appears that the military research officers are not partners in the alarmist scenario.
From AMAN's assessment it can be understood that even after the Iranian violations of the nuclear agreement in recent months - the sky has not fallen.

Even if it is not explicitly stated, at this stage it is about a few hundred kilograms of enriched uranium of a low civilian grade - and not a return to the situation that existed before the nuclear agreement of eight tons of enriched uranium using 19 thousand centrifuges.
The Iranian violations in the field of uranium enrichment are perceived in a relatively minor way and in a diplomatic, not a military, context.

It was reported that according to the research officers at the AMN, they were intended for the purposes of negotiations and exerting gradual pressure on the European partners to the agreement (Britain, France and Germany) to return the situation to normal.
That is, to repel the unilateral sanctions imposed by the US, or alternatively, to accumulate bargaining chips for a future nuclear agreement.
Kochavi and Netanyahu in military exercises in Carmel, this year Elad Gershgoran.
AMAN's assessment does not identify an Iranian acceleration to develop nuclear weapons.
In addition, Iran has not canceled its commitment to the nuclear agreement.
Signs of a moderate realist approach in AMN can also be found in what is not included in the annual assessment.
Amn does not talk about the possibility of nuclear weapons in the plutonium orbit.

This, out of awareness of the important clause that continues to exist in the nuclear agreement - according to which Britain and China will build a new heavy water reactor in Arak (in place of the old and dangerous reactor that was dismantled as part of the agreement) in such a way that it will not be possible to produce plutonium for a bomb.

Equally, it is a shame that the UN did not point out in its briefings that even with regard to the violation that is perceived as the most significant in Iran's series of violations in the field of uranium enrichment - the resumption of activity at the Purdue facility - it is not a return to the period before the nuclear agreement, that is, to the same underground "space of immunity" in which Uranium enrichment to 20%, which is the fast track to high military enrichment.
Only two-thirds of the thousand centrifuges at Purdue returned to enrich uranium but at a low civilian grade, unlike in the past.
The remaining third is intended for continued civilian isotope research and not for uranium enrichment.
The research was done as part of the activities of an international research center led by Russia, as stipulated in the nuclear agreement.
It should be emphasized that IAEA inspectors are regularly in Purdue.
We can summarize and say that the evaluation of Amn flooded the institutional discourse with tunes that we haven't heard in a long time.
Not only technical intelligence on "hard" quantitative facts and routine alarmist forecasts, but also analysis that takes into account "soft" qualitative elements of diplomacy and international art.

The complex analytical observation through which IAM tries to follow closely the latest developments regarding the nuclear agreement, and especially the tense dialogue between Iran and the three European signatories to the agreement - indicates that Iran is not rushing to the bomb.
This is in marked contrast to Netanyahu's stated position and his negative attitude towards the diplomatic route and the nuclear deal.
In his eyes, this is a replay of the Munich Agreement in 1938.
The prime minister and the military establishment do not see eye to eye on the Iranian nuclear issue.
The conceptual difference presented here will have an impact on the assessment of future developments and Israel's ways of responding.
For example, regarding the scenario of a pre-emptive war that Netanyahu contemplated in his speech on Memorial Day for the Yom Kippur War.

New research: the brain's immune system is able to stop the spread of deadly cancer

A new study by Tel Aviv University, published today (Monday) in the prestigious journal "Nature Communication", found that activating the brain's immune system against the deadly cancer glioblastoma, makes it possible to curb the spread of cancer cells in the body.
The research is considered groundbreaking and according to the researchers, may bring about a significant turn in the fight against brain cancer.
Early in the study, the researchers identified a failure in the brain's immune system that increases the division and spread of glioblastoma cancer cells instead of inhibiting them.

The failure results from the secretion of a protein in the brain called P-Selectin (SELP) with the help of which the immune system performs the opposite action and allows the penetration of the cancer cells into the brain tissue.

In the next step, the researchers were able to inhibit the secretion of the protein - and showed that by inhibiting the SELP it is possible to neutralize the "failure" in the immune system, returning it to a normal working path and thus stopping the spread of the incurable cancer.

In the next step, Prof. Sacchi-Painero and her team inhibited each of the proteins to try and isolate the one protein that allows the cancerous tumor to "enslave" the brain's immune system for its purposes - and spread.
In this way, the researchers found that it is a protein called SELP that disrupts the function of the immune system and accelerates glioblastoma tumors.
After the researchers inhibited the SELP on the tumor samples from the patients, they noticed that the tumors stopped dividing, stopped moving, and stopped being invasive.
The researchers obtained the same results both in tumors in model animals and in 3D models.

Subsequently, an RNA sequencing analysis was also performed at the single cell level, in collaboration with the laboratory of Dr. Assaf Medi from the Department of Pathology at the Faculty of Medicine at Tel Aviv University, and there, too, a decrease in the cancerous properties of the cells and activation of the immune system against the spread of the tumor was detected in cases where the SELP was silenced and the connection between the microglia and the glioblastoma cells was disrupted, which led to the inhibition of the cancer progression in the brain.

The research included an international team of researchers led by Prof. Ronit Sachi-Painero, who is the head of the Cancer Biology Research Center and the head of the Cancer and Nanomedicine Research Laboratory at the Sackler Faculty of Medicine of Tel Aviv University.

For the purpose of the study, the researchers collaborated with brain surgeons from the Ichilov Hospital and brain surgeons from Johns Hopkins University and the Lieber Institute in the United States.

"We wanted to know why the immune system in the brain is not doing its job," said Prof. Sachi-Painero, who added: "Therefore, we tested the interactions between the immune system cells in the brain and the glioblastoma cells in tumors that had just been removed from patients.
To our surprise, we found that not only that the microglial cells do not act to inhibit the cancer cells, they play a decisive negative role in their division, spread and mobility."
Prof. Sacchi-Painero emphasized that the new research may have life-saving therapeutic implications.
According to her, by coincidence, these days a second phase clinical trial is being conducted to inhibit SELP for a completely different purpose, to treat pain in sickle cell anemia.

Prof. Sacchi-Painero said she hopes that since the SELP-inhibiting treatment has been shown to be safe for use in humans, it will pave the way for a relatively quick approval of a clinical trial to re-label the treatment for glioblastoma.
The new study was funded by the Israel Cancer Research Fund (ICRF), the European Research Council (ERC), the Kahn Foundation, the Cancer Society and the National Science Foundation.

A cure for Corona also helps to save patients with this dangerous condition
Not many people are familiar with this medical condition, but for doctors in hospitals in Israel and around the world, it is one of the most frightening and dangerous scenarios.

Now a new drug, researched at Hadassah Hospital, offers for the first time an effective and life-saving treatment for the phenomenon. , or sepsis in Hebrew, is a condition that develops in the body due to a significant infection, and it may quickly deteriorate into a life-threatening condition and even death.

This clinical condition - in which the body reacts in an "excessive" way to a bacterial infection - brings more than 20 thousand people to the hospitals in Israel every year, and about 20 to 30 percent of them die from it.

Although it is a common and very dangerous phenomenon, until now the world of medicine deals with sepsis with the help of antibiotics and supportive care only, and for years researchers have been looking for an additional treatment that will really help patients who suffer from life-threatening sepsis.
Last week, significant progress was made in the field, when a drug called "Alostra" showed very encouraging data in the treatment of sepsis.

The drug was developed and researched at the Hadassah Hospital, in collaboration with Enlivex, under the leadership of Prof. Dror Mbaruch, director of the Internal Medicine Department and the Corona Department at Hadassah.
The study was published in the journal FRONTIERS IN IMMUNOLOGY.
If the name of this drug sounds familiar to you, you are not wrong.
"Alostra" is used today to treat severe corona patients (those experiencing cytokine storm).
It is in the course of a controlled study as a treatment for Corona, and recorded success in two studies that took place in hospitals in Israel.
How does alostra work?

In the early days of the corona epidemic, there was a lot of talk about cytokine storm - a broad concept that groups together several inflammatory conditions in which there is damage to the regulation of the functioning of the immune system.

This leads to a life-threatening systemic inflammatory condition, which includes a sharp increase in cytokines, which are proteins associated with an inflammatory response that cause excessive activation of inflammatory cells.
The result of this excessive activation ranges from a febrile illness accompanied by weakness to a multi-system injury that can lead to death.
Similar to corona, also in cases of sepsis a cytokine storm occurs in the body which can lead to death.

Prof. Mbaruch explained that the new drug "was born when I was interested in understanding what happens to a dead cell in the body, how do you know it is dead, who does it come into contact with in the body, and how is it eliminated.

During the research, I discovered that when the body detects an amount of dead cells, it works to end inflammatory processes and calms cells called macrophages, which is what we are looking for when a person has a cytokine storm."
In other words, when the body detects an amount of dead cells, it acts as if the inflammatory process is over - and calms down.
Therefore, Prof. Mobaruch and his team developed a dying but stable cell, one that can be worked with.
"The cells are taken from a healthy donor, engineered in the laboratory in such a way that they reach the patient's bloodstream and moderate the cytokine storm," he added.

The cells that are taken from a healthy donor and engineered in the laboratory are injected into the patient's body, then curb the inflammation or cytokine storm that is very damaging to corona patients and patients suffering from sepsis. 10 patients with sepsis recovered thanks to the medicine.

The article, published as mentioned last week, presents the data the researchers arrived at with the help of the new drug, led by the lead researcher in the experiment, Prof. Van Heerden, director of the intensive care department at Hadassah Ein Kerem Hospital.
"We treated with the drug about ten patients, men and women between the ages of 50-80 who suffered from sepsis and came to intensive care.
They received the medicine and recovered with the help of the treatment," explains Prof. Mbaruch, "compared to patients with similar data historically in which we saw about 27 percent mortality."
The drug is now moving to a controlled clinical study, one that examines the use of the drug versus the use of a placebo.

An interpello, reports the IRS agency, is a request that a taxpayer may make to the IRS agency before implementing a tax-relevant behavior, in order to obtain clarification in relation to a concrete and personal case concerning the interpretation, application or disapplication of legal rules of various kinds relating to taxes.

Europe starts again from the Mediterranean to revive our South - by Romano Prodi The new government has brought Italy closer to the European Union, mending broken relations and reopening prospects that had been closed.
As a first consequence, interest rates on government debt were lowered and prospects opened for partial sharing of the migration problem with other European countries.
Instead, our public opinion and our government have not yet opened the debate on how to build a European policy that takes into account the dramatic situation in the Mediterranean.

Not only has Libya been on fire for eight years, but Algeria has entered an endless transition phase, Egypt is adding growing political tensions to its economic difficulties, and Tunisia is finding great difficulty in completing the democracy-building process.

Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union, European policy, partly as a result of the urgencies of history, has turned its attentions primarily toward the North and East: no sound strategy has been devised toward the Mediterranean.
Instead, this is a top priority for Italy.
Indeed, we cannot expect to solve the problems of our South if it has only tension, conflict and misery on the other side of the sea.
Yet we are so far away from this goal that we do not even realize how much our relations with the countries on the southern shore have almost been nullified.
A century ago the number of Italians living in Egypt, Libya and Tunisia numbered in the hundreds of thousands.
Alexandria was a city with such a large Italian presence that Victor Emmanuel III fled there in exile precisely because it was the most Italian city outside our borders.
Our presence in all these countries made our language the most popular means of communication among sailors and traders on both shores.
The first step in directing European policy southward is in the development of a project shared by all countries bordering the Mediterranean.
In fact, our problems and difficulties are common not only with Spain, Greece, Cyprus, Malta, Slovenia and Croatia, but also with France.
Germany itself is realizing how much the weakness of the southern front in which the U.S., Russia and China fill our void comes at a cost, but only for their sole interest.
A European project for the Mediterranean must be based on some fundamental pillars.
The economic aspect is, of course, a priority and requires the implementation of more intensive trade relations and, above all, increased investment, which is now below expectations.
To remedy this state of affairs, we must first reexamine the idea of establishing a large development bank for the Mediterranean.

A bank in which decision-making powers are equally distributed among representatives of the two shores and which raises capital not only from Europe and Africa but also from other areas, starting with the Gulf countries.
This is to be complemented by the massive launch of a European project to establish a comprehensive renewable energy network.
A network that, while aiming to extend throughout Africa, certainly finds the most immediate possibilities for development in the Mediterranean countries.

However, one cannot limit oneself to cooperation in the economic field because human and cultural relations between the two shores of the Mediterranean have also weakened, which are the prerequisite for all forms of fruitful cooperation.
In this regard, more than 15 years ago, the European Commission put forward a proposal to build a network of mixed universities between North and South.

To be concrete: a university shared by Naples and Tunis or Palermo and Alexandria or Barcelona and Rabat, with equal numbers of professors and students from the North and the South and with the obligation of students to spend an equal number of years in both locations.
Nothing came of it because of the disinterest of Northern European countries.
I have listed only a few examples of a policy that cannot be only sectoral but must radically change relations between the two shores of the Mediterranean.
A policy shared at the European level but prepared and proposed by the countries on both sides, among which Italy is the indispensable driving force.

In fact, we must always keep in mind that it is not possible to think about the revival of the Mezzogiorno unless at the same time an area capable of creating development and cooperation is built around it.

"Our report on Italy makes it clear that there is still a long way to go in line with the Paris Agreement .
Companies' emission targets are not ambitious enough and few are officially based on science."
Although 60 percent of companies have already set emission reduction targets , in most cases they do not cover the entirety of their operations .
Another focal point for the ecological transition concerns cities.
In Italy 65 cities and regions have already declared a state of climate emergency .

Hardest hit are those in northern Italy where temperatures have risen over the past century by up to 1.2 degrees, according to the European Data Journalism Network organization's One Degree Warmer research.
The cities most at risk are Venice, Rome and Parma, part of the more than 3/4 of urban centers found to be vulnerable to heat waves , flooding and drought , according to the CDP report.

Only 60 percent of cities have an emissions reduction plan, less than one in four have completed a vulnerability assessment, and 12 percent have drafted a plan to adapt to the risks of climate change , such as in the areas of education , safety and planting to improve air quality.
In addition, the national climate change adaptation plan is still at the draft stage.
CPD's research was presented during the final days of the Madrid climate conference, which ends on Friday, Dec. 13.

COP25 is the last meeting of world leaders before 2020, when new climate action plans around the world must be determined to limit global warming to below 2 degrees and comply with the Paris agreements.

Pensions, from 2021 coefficients cut: here's what changes
Slight pension reduction coming for those who retire from work starting in January:
Starting in 2021, the new revision of the contribution amount transformation coefficients under the Dini reform was triggered.

Those who will retire starting in January with at least 67 years of age and a gross pension of about 2,000 euros per month, Uil calculates, will have a reduction in their check of about 10 euros per month compared to those who retired in 2020 with the same age and the same contribution amount.
The calculation is made on the assumption that one retires under a fully contributory calculation system as in the case of the woman's option.

For those retiring under the mixed system (i.e., those who had less than 18 years of contributions at the end of 1995), the cut will be smaller because there will be a portion of the pension calculated under the earnings-related system.

"The current mechanism," says Uil confederal secretary Domenico Proietti, "is penalizing for workers and disincentivizes them from staying at work, in stark contrast to the principle underlying the contributory system.
Postponing, in fact, access to retirement runs the danger of seeing one's contribution amount calculated with more unfavorable coefficients."

"The automatic revision of the coefficients for calculating pensions using the contributory system," says CISL Confederal Secretary Ignazio Ganga, "should be revised and become the subject of discussions with trade unions, as originally provided for in the 1995 Dini law.

The coefficient revision triggered in 2021 is the fifth since the Dini reform and the contribution system came into effect (the first was in 2010, then in 2013, 2016 and 2019) and will remain in effect until the end of 2022 .
The reduction in coefficients, linked to increases in life expectancy, was smaller this year than in past years.
In practice, those who retire at age 67 will multiply their contribution amount by 0.05575 in 2021 instead of 0.05604 in 2020 to get their annual check.
Those who leave at age 65 will multiply it by 0.05220 instead of 0.05245 (it was at 0.06136% until 2009).
In the logic of the contributory system, increasing life expectancy increases, at the same age of leaving work, the time in which the pension is received and thus the monthly amount is reduced.
Uil calculates that with a pension of 1,500 euros gross per month, at age 67 there is an annual loss of 101 euros with the change from 19,614 euros annually in 2020 to 19,513 in 2021.
The loss is naturally structural.

With a pension of about 2,000 gross per month, the difference between those retiring at age 67 in 2020 and 2021 is 136 euros, while with a pension of 2,500 gross per month, the annual difference still at age 67 for exit is 170 euros .

By leaving work toward retirement at a lower age, such as 62, one loses about 70 euros gross per year this year compared to last year for those with 1,500 euros per month of pension, 94 for those with 2,000 euros gross, and 117 for those with about 2,500 euros gross.

In Molise and Calabria automatic Irap and Irpef increases
Increased the rate of IRAP by 0.15 percentage points, and the rate of the regional income tax surcharge by 0.30 percentage points for taxpayers in Molise and Calabria.

In fact, the two regions led by Donato Toma and Jole Santelli have again for 2019 failed to meet the targets set by the health care deficit recovery plans, and therefore for 2020 the fiscal automatisms required by law will be inexorably triggered.

This is reported in the July 1, 2020 release of the Finance Department of the Ministry of Economy and Finance published on the institutional website www.finanze.it and the press release of the Internal Revenue Service published the same day on the website www.agenziadelleentrate.it in the "Press Room" section.

The communiqués were issued precisely for the purpose of publicizing the conclusions of the work of the Table for the Verification of Compliance and the Standing Committee for the Verification of Essential Levels of Care, whose task is precisely to monitor the implementation of the health deficit recovery plans of the regions that are contained in specific agreements signed with the regions.

In fact, said technical bodies, at their meetings on May 18, 2020 and May 25, 2020, were able to ascertain that in fiscal year 2019 neither the Molise region nor the Calabria region met the targets set in their respective health plans, resulting in the determination of a health deficit.

As was the case last year, therefore, the conditions required by Article 2, Paragraph 86, of Law 191 of 2009 for the automatic application of the surcharge were met: by 0.15 percentage points for the rate of IRAP; by 0.30 percentage points for the rate of the regional IRPEF surcharge.

Thus, these percentages are added to the existing rates in accordance with the procedures set forth in Article 1, Paragraph 174, of Law No. 311 of 2004 and end up making the tax burden significantly heavier on the citizens of the two regions, who, paradoxically, feel the burden of health care inefficiencies more than others.

In giving instructions on how to apply the rate increases, the Internal Revenue Service highlighted that the IRAP increase will affect the IRAP advance payment for 2020, which must be determined - with the historical method, assuming as the tax for the previous period the one determined by applying the 2019 rate already including the 0.15 percentage point increase; - with the forecast method, assuming as the reference tax the one determined by applying the tax rate increased by 0.15 percentage points to the expected value of production.

Regarding the increase in the rates of the regional income tax surcharge in the announcement of the Internal Revenue Service, it is specified that the increase of 0.30 percentage points for the 2020 tax year takes effect in the year 2021.

However, in relation to employees who terminate employment during the year, employers shall withhold, at the time of adjustment, the amount of the 2020 regional surtax applying the increased rate, and that of the remaining installments of the 2019 regional surtax, to which the previous rate applies.

So in case of termination of employment occurred during 2020, tax withholding agents will have to apply: the increased rate equal to 2.03 percentage points for the payment of the regional surtax with reference to the Calabria Region; however, for the Molise Region, the increased rates are provided on the basis of income brackets.

Welcome to the Pliocene climate
Three million years ago Antarctica was covered by trees and the temperature higher by 3-4 degrees.
Today for the first time we have reached the carbon dioxide levels of that era.
German scholars discovered this by studying the very ice of the South Pole.
Greenhouse gas emissions, meanwhile, continue to break records in defiance of agreements.
The only positive example: Germany
The last time this happened was in the Pliocene.
Three million years ago Antarctica was green, covered by trees, the world was 3-4 degrees warmer and the seas 15-20 meters higher.
Today we are back to the same level of carbon dioxide as at that time, when homo was not yet born: 410 particles per million.
Researchers noticed this by digging ice cores in Antarctica.
Deep down, the ancient part of the cap indeed retains tiny particles of the gases of the past.
For climate scientists, diving into that white blanket is like flipping backward through a history book.
By drawing their sample, researchers at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research have drawn little reassuring line between us and the Pliocene.
Their research is on For German researchers, at this rate Antarctica's color change will only be a matter of time.
The increase in carbon dioxide began roughly in 1750 (the conventional birth date of the Industrial Revolution) from about 280 particles per million.
In 1958, when measurements began, we were at 315.
In 2013 we crossed the 400 bar, with the average temperature of the planet increasing by one degree, and Nasa estimates a value of 450 by 2040.
The British newspaper The Guardian decided to publish carbon dioxide levels measured by the Mauna Loa station in Hawaii on its weather forecast pages.
Since the end of the Pliocene (1.6 million years ago), never had the thermometer marked more than two degrees higher than before the Industrial Revolution.
If greenhouse gas emissions continue like this," the scholars continue, "the 1.5-2 degree warming limit set by the Paris agreements will surely be exceeded.
In fact, it will probably be as low as 3 degrees, with the sea 50 centimeters higher by the end of the century.
Emissions should be stopped, scientists warn and international agreements dictate.
Instead, exactly the opposite is happening.
In 2018, three more particles per million added to the haul already so well represented in the atmosphere.
Three of the four pollution records were recorded in the past four years, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) reports.
According to the U.S. agency in charge of climate monitoring, the rate of greenhouse gas accumulation is 100 times higher than at the end of the last ice age, between 11,000 and 17,000 years ago.

In this landscape of discouragement and helplessness, a ray of sunshine came from The German government let it be known that it managed to reduce its emissions by 4.2 percent in 2018-not unique but rare except for countries in economic recession.
Of course, the milder climate helps northern countries, which do not have large consumption for air conditioning in summer.
"But on our result," explained Environment Minister Svenja Schulze, "weighed the increased use of sun and wind as energy sources instead of coal, oil and gas.
Salaries, the effect of the latest Maneuvers:
Public workers' paychecks detract 30% from those in the private sector
Since the end of the contract adjustment freeze (2009-2015), public employees' salaries have benefited from two generous rounds of renewals.

The first, 2016-2018, inspired by the need to compensate for the loss of purchasing power for PA employees due to the freeze, resulted in a 6.1 percent increase in public wages per labor unit, compared with a 1.8 percent increase in the reference price index (RPI) over the same period.
In contrast, wages in the private sector over the three-year period grew by 2.2 percent, just above the increase in prices.

With the approval of the Budget Law (BBA) 2021, the chapter on contractual adjustments for the three-year period 2019-2021 also closed, under the banner of potentially more generous increases than those of the previous three-year period.

In fact, while ISTAT forecasts about the price index again indicate a small increase of 1.8 percent, the increase in wages per unit of work in the public sector compared to 2018 could reach 6.5 percent by the end of 2021.

This increase is composed of moderate growth in 2019 (+0.2 percent, source ISTAT) and rapid growth in the following years (+2.1 percent in 2020 and +4.1 percent in 2021), based on the estimates of the Technical Report to the 2020 BBL and the additional allocations of the 2021 BBL (Fig. 1).

The increase in public salaries in the current three-year period is thus mainly due to the allocations of the last two Budget Acts, with which a total of nearly 3.8 billion euros was allocated for the renewal of central government employees' contracts in 2021 (including 400 million with the latest BUD).

In addition to this allocation, again for 2021 alone, about another 2.9 billion must be considered, which local governments and the like will have to make up independently to renew their contracts in line with those of the central state.
The allocations just described have inevitably reversed the recent trend in the ratio of private to public wages.
In fact, after the freeze had brought this ratio just above 1.2 (wages in PA were 21.3 percent higher than private wages in 2015), the ratio could exceed 1.3 by the end of 2021 (Fig. 2).
The development of the wage ratio inevitably depends on the dynamics of private wages in 2020 and 2021.

However, even assuming sustained growth for private wages, above inflation and in line with the three-year period 2016-2018 despite the economic crisis ("low" scenario in Fig. 2), in 2021 wages in PA would still come in 30.2 percent higher than private wages.
In addition, if private wages stagnate in 2020 and 2021, this difference could rise to 32.1 percent ("high" scenario in Fig. 2), which is a similar level as in 2009.

In other words, the most recent contractual adjustments would bring public wages relative to private wages to a level above the average of recent decades (1.28 over the period 1980-2019) and relatively close to the level reached just before the contractual freeze (around 1.35 between 2008 and 2009). [1] Although union negotiations regarding the contract renewal for the current three-year period have not yet been concluded, the earmarked resources are final (the ongoing negotiations concern only the criteria for distributing these resources among public employees).
As a result, it would appear that wages in the public sector are on a sustained growth path well above inflation, which could bring them to levels similar to pre-bloc levels.
Tax havens, EU parliament wants to revise blacklist criteria
Review the criteria for getting a country on and off the blacklist of tax havens.
the European Parliament passed a resolution calling for changes to the system used to draw up the EU list of tax havens because it is "confusing and ineffective."
criteria should be added to ensure that more countries are considered tax havens and prevent a country from being removed from the list too quickly.

The EU list of tax havens, established in 2017, has so far had a "positive impact," explain the EU parliament, but it has "not lived up to its potential as the jurisdictions it currently contains cover less than 2 percent of global tax losses."
In the approved nonlegislative resolution, which completes the discussion with the Council Presidency and the Commission, the current system is described as "confusing and ineffective."
Members propose changes that would make a country's assessment process more transparent, consistent and impartial.
In particular, some criteria should be added to ensure that more countries are considered tax havens and prevent a country from being removed from the list too quickly.
EU countries should not be excluded from the analysis to see if they exhibit any tax haven characteristics, and those that fail this test should themselves be considered tax havens.

"By calling the EU list of tax havens 'confusing and inefficient,' the EP is telling it like it is," said the chairman of the parliamentary subcommittee on taxation issues (FISC), Paul Tang (S&D, NL).
"The list can be a valuable tool, but member states forgot something when they compiled it: actual tax havens.
In fact, the list is not getting better, it is getting worse.
Guernsey, the Bahamas and now the Cayman Islands are just some of the well-known tax havens that member states have taken off the list.
By refusing to adequately address tax evasion, national governments are disappointing the expectations of their citizens by more than 140 billion euros.

Especially in the current context, this is unacceptable. "For this reason, the EP condemns the recent removal of the Cayman Islands from the list and calls for greater transparency and stricter criteria.
You also have to look in the mirror: EU countries are responsible for 36 percent of tax havens."
The criterion for judging whether a country's tax system is fair or not needs to be revised and expanded to include additional practices and not just preferential tax rates.
The recent removal of the Cayman Islands from the list, while a 0% tax rate policy applies in the country, is proof enough of the shortcomings of the assessment system.
Among other proposed measures, MEPs call for all jurisdictions with a corporate tax rate of 0 percent or no tax on corporate profits to be automatically placed on the list of tax havens.
The removal of a country from the list should not be the result of purely symbolic tax system changes.
According to Members, for example, the Cayman Islands and Bermuda were removed from the list following the introduction of "minimal" changes and "weak enforcement measures."
Thus, the EP calls for stricter screening criteria.
All third countries should be treated and evaluated equally and using the same criteria, yet the current list shows otherwise.
The lack of transparency with which the list is compiled and updated is an additional concern.
Therefore, the list-making process must be formalized through a legally binding instrument.
Beach Party, WWF:
"No harm done, we said no to dozens of sites."
In recent weeks we have seen some controversy over the impacts of the Jova Beach Party.

So it is only fair to try to bring order by recounting the work that concert organizers with the help of WWF have turned into actions to have the least possible and still manageable impact with respect to each individual location.
First, all beaches within parks, reserves, sites of community inter esse and special protection areas were excluded.

Each concert area was evaluated by considering the surrounding 3-kilometer radius, including considering the influx of audience and spectator routes, using transennediated routes on existing roads guarded by dedicated personnel.

Beaches on which the presence (even occasional) of protected species (such as the Kentish plover) was possible have been monitored since spring, and in these locations, concert dates were chosen so as not to create interference.
After a thorough materials investigation, hundreds of thousands of recyclable or compostable beverage and food containers were specially produced.
For those beverages on which these containers were not usable, such as beer, specific analysis and "life cycle assessment" procedures were done to use 80 percent recycled plastic cups.

A separate discussion should be made about water for which, after verifying with the Ministry of the Interior the impossibility of introducing and using water bottles, aluminum packaging was opted for precisely to have more effective recycling.
Everywhere in the concert area there are islands for recycling collection, which is facilitated by specific procedures and assigned staff.
Finally, the ways in which the area is restored after concerts are very timely and ensure that in 24 hours the strand is perfectly clean and available.

For the Jova Beach Party concerts, analyses, protocols, and procedures were applied that the thousands of small- to medium-sized events that annually take place on our beaches generally do not have, and when they do have them, they are never as comprehensive and thorough.
This was made possible by a precise choice of Lorenzo measured against prescriptions derived from WWF's screening and analysis.
All beaches are not the same.

Precisely on the basis of this principle, in addition to those in protected areas, dozens of beaches were excluded from the choice of locations, despite the legitimate requests of numerous local authorities applying with organizers to host the concerts.

A beach abutting a breakwater in Ravenna or the harbor wall in Roccella, a shoreline like that of the Pietro Mennea seafront on which the city of Barletta overlooks, the Casabianca di Fermo beach bordered by roads and railroad as well as a front of buildings for residential use, the beach of Castel Volturno, with respect to which everyone recognizes a revaluation process that began with the first Jova Beach Party in 2019, nothing to do with the dunes of Circeo or Castel Porziano, Feniglia in Argentario or Torre Salsa in Sicily, just to name a few examples.
This is not to say that more man-made beaches have no environmental value but simply that impacts can more easily be controlled and absorbed.
Incidentally, in many cases, stretches of shoreline that are habitually busy and often occupied by beach establishments that suspend their activities for the occasion are used for the concerts.

The i mmage of a mechanical vehicle on a beach-which no one, including WWF, likes-cannot generate confusion between environmental impact and environmental damage, nor can it lead one to believe that the concept of reversibility has not been, upstream, scientifically evaluated.

If several criticisms made for some beaches in the 2022 edition reiterate the same arguments already used for those same beaches during the 2019 concerts, it means that environmental damage (then) did not occur and that the recovery of naturalness of those places that occurred in less than 3 years demonstrates that the impacts were more than reversible.

Draghi , in short, is likely to appear before Biden politically weakened both in terms of Italian domestic and European politics.

A glimmer that would allow Rome's Atlantic anchorage to be combined with our national interest.

In his talks with Biden tomorrow, Draghi is expected to ask the U.S. president for concrete U.S. help in strengthening NATO's southern flank with a view to stabilizing the Mediterranean and, in particular, Libya.
That's right: at first glance it might seem that these objectives have no bearing on the Ukrainian dossier.
But this is not the case.

First and foremost, the stabilization of Libya would ensure an increase in gas supply to the European Union-a scenario that would therefore make the EU itself less dependent on Russian energy and better able to dampen the economic backlash of sanctions.
All this would also avert the risk of dangerous short-circuits: recall that Algeria, which Italy recently turned to for gas supplies, has close relations with Moscow and Beijing.
Second, a stabilization of Libya would allow for a major blow to Russia, which, let us remember, holds significant influence over the eastern part of the North African country.

Finally, a stabilization of the Mediterranean would make it possible to cope more effectively with the Iranian threat-remember that Tehran's ballistic missile program continues to be of particular concern.
That same Tehran which, incidentally, turns out to be a close ally of Moscow.
It is therefore in light of these considerations that Draghi should call for a strengthening of NATO's southern flank and clear and concrete support to stabilize Libya.
Of course: as we said at the beginning, there is no shortage of difficulties.
And the premier himself, because of the divisions inherent in his majority, will arrive in Washington politically somewhat crippled.

Capital Group: the US financial cycle is approaching its peak

The U.S. financial cycle is approaching its peak, due to the effects of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, such as sharply rising commodity prices, slowing world trade, and increased uncertainty for households and businesses.
In addition, a more aggressive Fed pushes up the cost of mortgages.
Much now depends on real estate prices holding up, but double-digit growth is unlikely to go on for long.
Inflation at 40-year highs is among the factors weighing most heavily on the cycle, which may now be close to a downturn.

CREDIT GROWTH BRAKES Jens Søndergaard, currency analyst at Capital Group, believes it is difficult for a recovery factor to emerge as the Fed aggressively raises rates and predicts that in the absence of substantial private sector releveraging, credit growth is likely to slow further and enter negative territory during 2022.
It has happened before, during the last two peaks of the U.S. financial cycle in the late 1980s and between 2006 and 2007.
But according to the Capital Group expert, the financial cycle is not only at risk in the United States but also in other developed markets.

STOPPING DEBT EXPOSITS Considering the global nature of the recent inflationary surge and the central banks' liquidity drain, according to Søndergaard we are likely to see most financial cycles further approaching their peak or, even, the beginning of relative deleveraging, i.e., the unwinding of debt exposures, which would also be bad for equity markets.
But according to Capital Group, there is less risk of the trend culminating in a global credit crunch because banks' capital levels are much higher today than before the financial crisis.
But there is little doubt that most developed countries are firmly in the latter stages of their financial cycles.
IN EUROPE PEAK MAY HAVE ALREADY TOUCHED In the eurozone, the cycle may have already passed the peak.
Germany aside, there are no credit or housing booms, and soaring inflation makes an acceleration of private debt even more unlikely.
The German housing market has been performing quite well recently, but credit growth has begun to decline.
In 2020, peripheral countries experienced credit growth that is beginning to slow and may have been only a temporary effect of the pandemic.
REBASSING EFFECTS FOR THE EURO l all have bearish effects for the euro against the dollar.
The Eurozone financial cycle is weakening faster than the US financial cycle, the Fed is more aggressive than the ECB , which makes the real rate differential more favorable to the greenback.
Europe is also much more vulnerable to energy supply disruptions from Russia.

Broadening the horizon, according to Søndergaard, China's financial cycle has already passed its peak, having grown dramatically after the global financial crisis and received further impetus from the 2020 stimulus in response to the pandemic.
CHINA HAS HAD A HARD TIME MANAGING THE TREND Chinese authorities have struggled to manage orderly deleveraging.
Real estate prices and sales are in free fall, several real estate groups are grappling with significant credit stress, "zero COVID" policy lockdowns may continue for the rest of the year and beyond.
This would most likely weigh on already weak consumption, further depressing property sales and exacerbating rising unemployment.
These are all factors bound to cause further disruptions in supply chains and drag down global growth, with likely negative repercussions for Emerging Markets such as Vietnam, Malaysia and Brazil.
RECESSION NOT BY COURSE IMMINENT Compared to a year ago, Søndergaard's analysis concludes, several countries have approached or even surpassed their financial peaks.
Rising inflation and rates, the Chinese slowdown and the conflict in Ukraine are all fueling the trend.
In many countries, the gains in real estate prices that followed the pandemic appear increasingly vulnerable, while in advanced economies private debt growth is now flat.

Although the peak in the financial cycle does not necessarily signal an impending recession, it does portend a period of deleveraging potentially weighing on global growth, according to Capital Group.

Antitrust:
3.2 mln fine to Lyoness for pyramid selling.

The Antitrust Authority has sanctioned for 3.2 million euros the company Lyoness Italia Srl after finding that the promotion system used to spread among consumers a formula for purchasing goods with cashback (i.e., with the return of a percentage of the money spent at affiliated merchants) is unfair because it integrates a system with pyramidal characteristics, a case included by the Consumer Code among commercial practices in any case misleading.

The promotion scheme, using the pretext of the described advantage of cashback purchases, actually takes the form of recruiting a large number of consumers who are asked, after assuming the role of sales representative, to pay a particularly high entry fee to access the first commission level (amounting to 2,400.00 euros) and start their "career" as a Lyconet Premium Marketer.
Thereafter, they must recruit other consumers as well as make additional payments to confirm and progress in the "career."

The investigation carried out revealed that the possibility of obtaining a deferred discount on purchases in the form of cashback is actually a minor aspect of the economic volume generated by the Lyoness system (amounting to about 1/6 of total revenues).

In fact, the achievement of high levels of Shopping Points-the compensation plan's remuneration mechanism-is in essence only possible with payments of sums of money from participating consumers or from entities recruited by them.

As it turns out, numerous tens of thousands of consumers paid the aforementioned sums of money to enter, participate in and remain in the system, and only very few individuals actually succeeded in achieving significant positions.

In addition, the Authority has ascertained the misleading manner in which the characteristics, terms and conditions of the Lyoness promotion system are projected, aspects that are not adequately clarified both on the websites and at promotional events, as well as the absence on these websites of certain essential information required in distance selling, such as that on how to handle complaints, the right of withdrawal and the competent court.

Duties, #MeToo, genetically modified babies: all of China's censorship on WeChat
Most of all, the trade war with the United States.
But also health scandals, the #MeToo movement protests and the birth of the first genetically modified babies.

It's not just politics that the Chinese communist regime considers destabilizing, judging by the ranking of the top ten most censored topics in 2018 on WeChat, the all-purpose app where a billion of the Dragon's citizens chat and inform themselves.

The list was compiled by researchers at the University of Hong Kong, who monitored 4 thousand news channels: out of more than one million published posts, about 11 thousand were later deleted, one in a hundred.
That may not seem like much in a country that ranks last in the world for press freedom.

But to these must be added the issues blocked preemptively, even before publication, which is why, for example, the abolition of presidential term limits desired by Xi Jinping does not appear in the rankings.

Net of this distortion of perspective, the research reveals that the topic most obscured by the leadership last year was the all-out challenge with America: in addition to tariffs, sanctions against Zte and the arrest in Canada of Meng Wanzhou, the princess of the Huawei empire, were among the ten topics deleted.
A censorious punctiliousness behind which the report's authors read the regime's desire to defend, in the eyes of its citizens even before the world, China's image as a superpower.
Instead, many of the other themes are related to news incidents that have gone viral and embarrass the regime, exposing limitations and contradictions in the Chinese system.

One of the people's most heartfelt issues for example is that of health safety: thus news about the scandal of adulterated vaccines administered to thousands of children, or the medical liquor sold for years by one company as a miracle remedy, disappeared from WeChat.
Again, authorities made sure that there was no mention of the sudden downfall of Ye Jianming, a young oil entrepreneur arrested for bribery, or the maxi tax evasion blamed on movie star Fan Bingbing.

Finally, news stories related to the experiment of He Jiankui, the scientist who delivered the first babies with modified DNA, and those about the #MeToo movement at Peking University, where a student brought to light a case of harassment buried in omertà, were heavily censored.
Arguments that are not strictly political, but capable of inflaming public opinion and contrary to those "positive values" that the Communist Party believes the Web should help spread.

Overall, 2018 was a year of further tightening of Net freedom in China, marked by the appointment of a new head of the Internet Authority, peppered with new bans, and culminating in the closure of thousands of profiles of so-called "self media" journalists, commentators, or influencers who post their stories on social networks, especially WeChat.
"Mobile platforms are a priority," Xi Jinping said in a recent meeting with state media.
Hinting that 2019 will be even worse.

Draghi government, Moody's: improved outlook for use of EU funds
Mario Draghi's government "improves" Italy's prospects for "effective use of European funds."
Moody's says this, stressing that "long-term challenges" however remain .

Once the pandemic-related urgency eases, it will likely face "similar difficulties and political opposition to some structural reforms that we have observed with other governments in the past," Moody's notes.

The current political moment in Italy can be compared with the technical government led by Mario Monti in 2011-2013 : the existence of an EU aid package is, however, an important difference, Moody's notes, pointing out that the new government's pursuit of an economic reform program that will be subject to Brussels supervision is an equally important similarity.
"The latest Eurobarometer survey indicates that only 28 percent of Italians trust the EU, the lowest percentage among all 27 countries.

Having Mario Draghi as premier press for unpopular reforms is not without risks in the long term" , adds Moody's, according to which risks could include amplifying the anti-European populist tendencies that have emerged over the past decade.

For the rating agency, "once the urgency of the pandemic eases, the key challenge for the government will be to maintain the momentum behind the reforms and political support" for the changes: some parties or parliamentary groups "have for years actively opposed" some aspects of judicial and administrative reforms proposed by previous administrations.
It is then stressed that "the productive use of European funds will be inextricably linked to the success of the new government's economic reform agenda.
Administrative difficulties, especially in the Italian regions most in need of investment, have in the past hindered the absorption of European funds.

The change of government in Italy has positive credit implications in the short term, Moody's says, noting that under Draghi's leadership the plan Italy will present in Brussels "will likely include high-quality infrastructure projects that can strengthen the country's growth prospects."

"The Draghi government's agenda is likely to seek structural economic reforms to improve growth potential," Moody's adds, listing areas long identified by international organizations as those most in need of reform, among them administration, justice and the tax system.

Australian area airline Qantas has asked its managers to lend a hand, for three months, to the baggage department.

The company has asked a hundred managers to commit three to five days a week for the next three months as part of a "contingency plan" to relieve pressure on ground staff.

Qantas director of operations Colin Hughes explained that the airline is trying to manage the impact on airline logistics and ground passenger services caused by the large number of influenza and Covid-19 infections in what is a southern hemisphere winter.

Not only that, like many airlines, Qantas is struggling to cope with the spike in travel demand and demand: during the pandemic, when countries closed their borders, it grounded planes and thousands of employees, many of whom belonged to the ground staff themselves.
It now struggles to regain the quality of service it had before the pandemic.

A spokesperson confirmed the decision and explained that this is a usual initiative during busy periods (in April, during the Easter vacations, some 200 office managers were involved in airport logistics activities).
"It is clear to us that our operational performance has not lived up to our customers' expectations or the standards we expect," he added in a note.

After announcing the layoff of more than 1,600 ground workers, including baggage handlers, in November 2020 during the pandemic, the airline decided to outsource ground services, but the Federal Court of Australia held in two rulings, in 2021 and last May, that this measure was illegal.

Now the transport workers' union has criticized the measure announced by the company, which was privatized between 1993 and 1997, and said the "illegal" subcontracting of workers laid off during the pandemic did not work: "There are about 2,000 laid-off workers in 2020 who could do this (baggage handling) work.

It used to be the challenge of the free market, more or less regulated, against the planned, state-run economy.
Today the challenge is all internal to capitalism, seeking social harmony between the productive classes and those trudging in the last wagon.
In global terms, capitalism has done great good for humanity.

People in absolute poverty, almost the entire population of the planet at the beginning of the 1800s, have since declined in percentage, out of a growing population thanks precisely to less destitution, and then since 1970 also in absolute numbers, until two years ago when the Cricketers finally defeated poverty.
In this century, the distribution of wealth among countries has also shown signs of rebalancing.
In 2000, rich countries left just 20 percent of wealth to others, split between middle-income countries (14 percent) and low-income countries.
Fifteen years later, also aided by the 2007 financial bubble, the share of middle-income countries had risen to 22 percent and low-income countries had risen to 7 percent.
However, how much more or less wealthy a nation is than others remains an intangible index.

Much more important is to look at the distribution of wealth within the individual country: the Gini coefficient shows different values, the result of greater or lesser regulation and the degree of welfare in the respective economies.

Among rich countries, Italy has one of the most equitable wealth distribution ratios, along with Spain and Japan; more than France, Germany and the United Kingdom; far more than Sweden and the United States.
But we are still talking about a ranking that citizens care little about, since people live and perceive themselves within individual states.

When life gets complicated, because technological change, international competition, and perhaps a major crisis 2007/8 sweep away the balance, those who are worse off check two things: whether they were better off or worse off in the recent past and whether those around them are doing better or worse off, that is, whether the distribution of wealth has changed toward less or more equity.
Now, since the turn of the century, people in many OECD countries have seen it decline, although there are also significant exceptions, such as the United Kingdom and South Korea.
Italy got worse, seeing this coefficient increase by two percentage points to 0.58 in 2017.

According to a McKinsey study, a consulting firm, one of the causes at the European and global levels that have eroded wealth has been the combination of stagnant wages and rising housing prices well above the average level of inflation.
This is almost a quarter of household spending, by far the largest item, as much as food and transportation combined.
From 2002 to 2017, housing prices in the EU rose faster than overall inflation, by an average of 22 percentage points.

It is true that prices for clothing, furniture and leisure, 20 percent of spending, have plummeted, but this does not balance the home, which is neither renegable, nor compressible, nor even dilutable: its impact has been tremendous.
This is the same dynamic seen in the U.S., where in addition prices in health care have risen even higher.

Yet, Italians who say the financial situation of the average citizen has worsened compared to 20 years ago are 72 percent compared to 45 percent of Americans, despite the fact that the Gini coefficient has increased by 5 points for them, to 0.81 versus Italy's 0.58.
The fact is that disposable income has changed.
Average paying jobs have declined, in favor of jobs that pay very much or very little, that is, those salaries that are not enough to cover all expenses or contribute to retirement.
It has happened in all rich countries, but not to the same extent.
While average wage earners in Italy declined by about 11 percent, in America the decline was 7 percent.
Various populisms and regurgitations of communism have many causes, but the money, wealth and prospects that the system is able to offer affect and a lot.
This is the challenge of capitalism, and it is not easy.

The long end of the borderless Internet

To understand exactly the meaning and scope of the order Facebook received to stop bringing European users' personal data to the United States, which set off red flags not only in Menlo Park, where Zuckerberg is based, but throughout Silicon Valley, we have to go back almost a quarter of a century.
At the Davos summit in 1996: it was looking bad for the powerful of the earth, the signs of what would become the "no global" protests were all there.
The most exciting moment had been when Shimon Peres and Yasser Arafat had shared the stage giving everyone hope that peace in the Middle East was indeed possible.

Probably to lighten the program, the organizers had arranged a session with some Internet pioneers: the World Economic Forum website had just been launched, and they must have thought it would be fun to hear from the gurus of the "information highways" (that's what they called the Net).
Among them was John Perry Barlow.

A poet, lyricist for the Grateful Dead, and recently deceased Internet activist, Barlow had arrived at Davos with a problem: he had been commissioned to write a text for a book that was to chronicle 24 hours in "cyberspace" (an expression hardly anyone uses today to refer to what we do online).
He worked on it overnight and finished it at dawn on February 8, but it was so radical that the book's publisher rejected it.
Barlow then introduced him to the Davos audience who must have found him very picturesque.
It begins thus, "Governments of the Industrial World, weary giants of flesh and steel, I come from Cyberspace, the new seat of Mind...."

That text is called the "Declaration of Independence of Cyberspace" and in apocalyptic tones it basically says that national governments have no sovereignty in this new space called the Internet: "On behalf of the future we ask you who are the past to leave us alone.
You are not welcome among us.
You have no power in the place where we meet."

That text set the standard, it is among the most quoted when discussing the history of the Internet, but things have not been that way from any point of view: the net has not become that place where everyone is free and equal consecrating "a more humane and honest civilization," but platforms have emerged that have imposed their own rules and a business model that uses our personal data, while hatred, disinformation and pornography have found fertile ground in algorithms that seem to be made specifically to showcase our worst sides.
Meanwhile, national governments have been waking up and digitally reconstructing the boundaries of the real world for a few years now.

Brick by brick, law by law, one ruling at a time. , as the MIT magazine calls it, or rather of "digital sovereignty," the successful attempt to impose even in what used to be cyberspace the rules of "meatspace," as Barlow called it, the space of real life, of flesh-and-blood people.

The signs are growing: Trump first declaring war on Huawei over 5G and then on a seemingly innocuous app like Tik Tok to prevent Americans' data from ending up in China; the European Union initiating major litigation even before the data move to impose tax and competition rules on Silicon Valley; while countries with authoritarian regimes enact increasingly restrictive regulations on the Internet, shutting it down when they want, reopening it to censor it, spying on dissidents.
Perhaps it was inevitable, it is probably even right, but it is the end of a utopia and it is not something that started today.
Ten years after his Declaration, Barlow was asked to take stock of how it had gone.
It was 2006, there were no social media yet.
Yet the wind had already changed quite a bit.
The old poet honestly acknowledged this but also said that it was not over, that he had not lost hope that the Internet would create a better world.
It won't be paradise, he said, there will still be us humans with our flaws, but it will be better than all that were there before.
One day, he concluded, it will be so.

Minimum corporate tax of 15 percent.

During the first reading in the Senate, the provision would also be amended by making it so that otherwise unrelated companies under common ownership of an investment fund do not have their aggregate profit for the purposes of the $1 billion threshold.
Excise tax on corporate share buybacks.

Network slicing 5G: Ericsson, TIM and Comau experiment with the "factory of the future"
Develop 5G solutions that can meet the rigorous requirements of important vertical industries such as Industry 4.0, Transportation, and Energy, following a field-testing approach.
This is the goal of the EU-funded 5Growth (5G-enabled Growth in Vertical Industries) project .
Launched in 2019, the project is another step forward in the long-standing partnership between Ericsson, TIM and Comau .

Thanks to TIM and Ericsson's deployment of a 5G network at Comau's Turin facility, three new applications were, in fact, fielded to demonstrate the benefits of the new technology in an industrial environment, particularly those derived from the network's slicing functionality.
"Network Slice," - Tim explains in a note - are virtual logical network portions of 5G, which support different application cases with special characteristics and requirements.

The same 5G physical network can then have multiple slices, each dedicated to specific services or customers, thus offering greater flexibility, efficient use of network resources, and more opportunities for enterprises that in turn can use differentiated services with specific speed, latency, and reliability requirements.

The first use case under experimentation involved the movement of a robot that, through an ultra-low latency radio link, produces a digital replica where the movement of the mechanical robot and respective virtual renderings are perfectly synchronized.
Moreover, thanks to the constant updating of the central system, the best production process can be decided according to the working parameters.
The second application is related to real-time monitoring of industrial assets .
Data are acquired from various sensors and sent to an application that uses them to improve predictive maintenance planning, production processes, and quality.
By integrating with Comau's digital platform "in.Grid," any deviation from normal operation can be recognized effectively and timely.

Similarly, remote assistance and access to cloud-based resources, such as high-definition video and real-time connections with augmented reality devices, greatly reduce repair time in case of failure.

The third case involved the application of immersive telepresence in an advanced remote service scenario, in which maintenance personnel present at the site are assisted remotely by an expert in order to resolve a fault, taking advantage of both augmented reality (AR) and digital tutorials.
In fact, thanks to the high bandwidth capacity of 5G, it is possible for the operator to share what he sees in real time with experts remotely, with benefits on time and cost.

"We are proud to support the growth and evolution of the industrial market and digital ecosystem, which undoubtedly represent huge opportunities to produce innovative solutions," says Daniele Franceschini, Tim's head of Innovation.

With partners such as Comau and Ericsson, we can ensure the development of new services and networks that can be configured with a high level of real-time security to create customized business scenarios such as those related to Industry 4.0.
With our expertise we will contribute to digitalization by providing solutions that improve the production processes of businesses and public administration."

"Comau is committed to defining a new automation paradigm, which involves the use of external sensors to detect parameters within automated production environments and to collect the sensed data in real time in a central brain.

The information gathered is used to automatically define and optimize the tasks to be performed by the machines in a flexible and efficient manner," explains Alessandro Piscioneri, Digital Solutions and Services Segment leader.

The 5Growth project, which we developed in close collaboration with two prominent partners, such as Tim and Ericsson, has allowed Comau to directly field test the value of private 5G technology as an enabling factor for this innovative architecture, especially in a mobile robotics context."

"Together with Tim and Comau," comments Alessandro Pane, R&D director, Ericsson in Italy, "we have demonstrated some applications that are indispensable in a rapidly changing manufacturing environment, where production needs to be safer, more flexible and faster.
Network slicing will play a crucial role in creating innovative services, accelerating the digital transformation of all enterprises.

Thanks to advanced technologies for efficient management of network resources, developed in Ericsson's R&D centers in Italy, operators can thus realize new use cases for different industries and exploit new market opportunities."

Silver and copper for mask that destroys Covid-19 virus
It not only protects against Covid, but also destroys the virus.
To look at it, it looks like a cotton mask, but it is in the central part that the secret of the solution lies: silver and copper nanolayers deposited on polypropylene.
This new material is called SakCu and was developed by the Materials Research Institute of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam).
Leading the team of researchers was Sandra Rodil, who explained how Sak, in the Mayan language, means silver, while Cu is the acronym that on the periodic table identifies the element copper.
These metals, reads the Unam journal, have been used for antiviral, antibacterial and even antifungal properties.
When the pandemic appeared, researchers had verified that copper surfaces were the ones that most rapidly reduced the concentration of the viral load responsible for Covid-19 infection.
Therefore, a silver-copper mixture was thought to be used to form a nanolayer between 30 and 40 nanometers thick, thus offering dual protection against viruses and bacteria.
In collaboration with Hospital Juárez de México, the Unam team demonstrated that the silver-copper nanolayer inactivates Sars-CoV-2.

Drops with the virus, taken from Covid-19-positive patients, were placed on the silver-copper film deposited on polypropylene, and it was observed that, depending on the viral concentration, different results were obtained: if it was high, the virus decreased by more than 80 percent within eight hours, while if the viral load was low, no virus RNA was detected after two hours.
Upon contact with the silver-copper nanolayer, in fact, the Sars-CoV-2 membrane ruptures and its RNA is damaged.
In collaboration with the National Institute of Rehabilitation, cytotoxicity tests were conducted on the surface of polypropylene with silver-copper deposition.
Researchers rule out risks to people who will use this mask, especially for direct skin contact.

Once the antiviral function was verified and the cytotoxic risk was excluded, the silver-copper nanolayer was used to make a face mask from natural and reusable fabrics to reduce the problem of mask disposal.
The mask has outer and inner layers of cotton and a filter interlayer of polypropylene coated with SakCu, which can be washed up to 10 times without losing its biocidal properties.
These masks also have a filtration efficiency of 50 percent for aerosol-like particles and 80 to 90 percent for 2.5-micron particles.

Banksy's nativity scene is in Bethlehem, but the comet star is the hole left by a grenade
Among the leading contemporary authors of "artivism," Banksy on Christmas Eve returns to express with Christian symbolism his view of the conflict between Palestinians and Israelis.
And again he chose Bethlehem, in the West Bank, to propose a modified Nativity-as he called it on Instagram-likely to stir up quite a bit of controversy.
At the entrance to the Walled-off, the hotel that opened in 2017 directly across from Israel's protective wall, the mysterious British artist had the Bethlehem Scar installed.
It is a small manger, an icon of the Christian Nativity, leaning against a piece of the Wall of Protection pierced at the top by a grenade or mortar shell.
That jagged hole, however, takes on the shape of the Comet Star hovering above Mary and Joseph watching over Jesus warmed, as tradition dictates, by an ox and a donkey.
The words peace, freedom, love are graffitied on the background wall in English and French.
A scar of shame said, quoted by the media, Walled-Off Hotel director Wissam Salsaa.
A scar that," he continued, "should bring shame on all those who support the wall and Israel's occupation of the Palestinian Territories.
It is a terrific and different way to talk about Bethlehem, to push people to think more about the way we live here.

Israeli media recalled that the protective barrier-part concrete and part not-was built by the army during the Second Intifada in 2000 to stop Palestinian suicide attacks.The International Court of Justice declared the barrier's construction illegal in 2004.
Israel says the wall continues to protect the state from attacks by assailants from the West Bank.
Palestinians, on the other hand, consider the barrier one of the most outrageous symbols of the Israeli occupation.

Just down the road, the Walled-Off Hotel in Bethlehem-whose launch slogan was the hotel with the worst view in the world-has over time become a landmark not only in welcoming tourists, with its 10 rooms partly designed by Banksy himself and others, but also from a purely political point of view.
Housed inside are an art gallery and also a museum that tells the story of the Wall and the conflict.
In addition, there is the possibility of equipping oneself with stencils that can be used to draw or write on the controversial wall.

Banksy for that matter is no stranger to forays into the conflict: in 2007 he left several drawings on the Bethlehem wall, including the famous one, in inverted parts, of a little girl inspecting an Israeli soldier her arms in the air and her rifle resting next to him.
In 2005, however, he had made nine different drawings using the stencil technique: these included a ladder leaning against the wall and a little girl being carried aloft by balloons.
Banksy's intention is to highlight the impact of the wall on Palestinian lives.

"I know Putin well, he doesn't respect any rules."

Bombing rages on in Kiev, but Valérie Pécresse, French presidential candidate for the Republicans, the moderate, neo-Gollist right wing, scrambles for votes from one Normandy village to the next, close to the icy waters of the English Channel.

Valérie Pécresse is a former top of her class: graduating high school two years early, graduating from Hec (a sort of French-style super Bocconi) and Ena, the hothouse of the country's elite.
He even speaks Russian, fluently .

As a teenager, a fan of Tolstoy and Dostoevsky, she began studying that language and went to spend long periods in the summer camps of the Soviet Communist Youth (she who came from an upper-class family in Versailles, strictly Gaullist, but also open-minded and nonconformist).
Thus, inevitable and unlikely, the talk, in the rolling hills of Normandy, falls on Vladimir Putin.
Have you ever met him?
"Yes.

Who is Vladimir Putin today?
"For a time I also worked at the French Embassy in Moscow.

We also need to supply the Ukrainians with weapons before it is too late.

Macron was banking on his personal relationship with the Russian president... "But in fact he had already been fooled by him in the past.

Who could mediate with Putin?

You have taken very tough positions on immigration in recent weeks, sometimes contradicting those that have been yours in the past.

He criticizes other candidates for their past support of Putin... "There are some who have defended Russia's position, aligned themselves with its positions, and are funded by Russian interests.
